It works four times in five, the best odds out there, and it works because of what is left of this animal. Carry the pole anyway when you cross:
the other cat
in that fen does not hide and will not be fooled by a coat.

loreStory: It is far along. What thins out of a hunting cat goes in an order, and the order is the country first, then the prey, then the difference between the prey and anything else with roughly that outline. What it still holds, perfectly, is one silhouette and the conviction that the silhouette is food. It has gone at a barrow with a sack on it, at a bundled coat, and at its own reflection in flat water, which is the one people find hard to watch.

The low ford was kept for years by a woman who fed it. Not sentiment; she had worked out that a fed one lies up and a hungry one comes to the causeway, and she would rather buy the crossing than defend it. She thinned in her turn and went Quiet, and the cat is still on that stretch, and there is still meat on the flat stone by the water most weeks. The walkers took the job over between them. Not one of them can tell you her name.

monsters.name: Mireglare
monsters.lore: Its stare bores through the fen-mist and burns. Hunters who meet those still eyes are found lit from within.
monsters.loreDesc: The fen's other cat, and it does not hide. It walks into the firelight, looks at every face in turn, and goes.

loreStory.t: It is nothing like
the stalker

. Squat, heavy through the shoulder, blunt in the face, and with no interest at all in cover. It comes to a fen fire, sits down inside the light where everyone can see it, and looks at the people. One at a time. It takes as long as it takes. Then it gets up and goes back out into the dark.

loreStory: Hunters tell the stare as an attack, which is what people do about anything that will not stop looking at them, and the fen has a whole vocabulary for what those eyes are supposed to do to you. Watch it happen twice and the story goes flat. It is not doing anything to you. It is checking. Face, then the next face, losing interest at each one, and it has been working through faces for longer than anyone at that fire has been dead.

loreStory.t: Hearn

sits still for it. He is the one man on that circuit who has been looked over by something worse, and he will not say a word about that, but he will say this: you let it finish. Turning your face away from a thing that is looking for somebody is a rudeness he is not willing to commit. The others follow his lead now, so the fire goes quiet for a minute when the cat comes in, twelve people holding their chins up to be inspected by an animal, and then it leaves and they carry on.

monsters.name: Stumpling
monsters.lore: A stump that woke one spring. It hauls itself along on root-legs and lashes at anyone who treads on its moss.
monsters.loreDesc: A stump with no tree behind it, walking on root-legs. It does not mind you coming. It minds you leaving.
loreStory: Every village that ever was had one: the stump at the wood's edge where you walked people to say goodbye. You carried their bag that far and no farther, and they sat on it to retie a boot, and then they went, and you stood by the stump until you could not see them. A thousand villages, a hundred thousand goodbyes, all of them remembered hard by the people left standing there — and in Nangijala that much remembering, pooled in one shape, eventually stands up.

So mind the one thing every handler tells you and no field guide bothers to: a Stumpling will let you walk right up. It goes for your back. The lashing starts when you turn and go, because going is the only thing that was ever done to it, and somewhere in all that borrowed remembering it has decided, wordlessly, with nobody inside it to decide, that this time it will not be left.

loreStory.t: Sigrun
will not crack them. She does the trade's other work all day and charges double to anyone who brings her one of these still whole, hoping she'll change her mind. The stone inside is
blood-natured

— it feeds your wounds shut while you fight, holding on to you the way the stump holds on to everyone — and she says a thing that keeps its grip that well should be allowed to keep it. People assume she is joking. People have not watched her leave her smithy, at the end of a market day, by the long way around the one that stands at the east fence.

monsters.name: Gravecharger
monsters.lore: A war-mount that refused to fall with its rider. It still charges the enemy line, centuries after the war.
monsters.loreDesc: It would not fall when its rider did. It still charges a line that is not there, in horns no horse ever grew.
loreStory: Nothing that ever grazed a field had that head. A horse's skull as far as the brow, then two great curled ram's horns on it, a ridge of bare spine standing out of the hide, something red down in the sockets. It did not look like that in life. It looks like that because it was the last thing a great many frightened men saw properly, and frightened men are poor witnesses, and enough of them told it the same way for long enough that the telling won. Set in the bone above the eyes is a small gold boss, all that is left of a head-piece somebody buckled onto it every working morning.

loreStory.t: The war is in nobody's book.
Bettany

has asked at every fire on her circuit for a banner, a year, a river, a reason, and come back with none of it — everyone who could have told it has gone Quiet, and it was never told often enough to hold. What survives of the entire business is one horse that will not stop, and a set of horns it never had.

It does not charge people. It charges lines. Two of you standing together are furniture; six in a row are a shield-wall, and it comes at the middle of the row at a flat gallop and does not check. Most of the work at a fire is done in rows — wood passed hand to hand, buckets, a line walking the ground abreast at first light.
Hearn

teaches everyone who works that country the same three sentences, and teaches them as orders, because an order is the only way he knows to say a thing fast enough. Break up. Stand apart. It is not coming for you, it is coming for the row.

monsters.name: Rotjaw
monsters.lore: Too stubborn to stay buried. Its crooked jaw hangs loose, grinning at a joke told before it died.
monsters.loreDesc: A dog that would not stop waiting. Its crooked jaw hangs loose, grinning at a joke told before it came.
loreStory: The joke was not funny. A long one about a neighbour and a borrowed ladder, with the same wrong pause in the middle every time, told to the same dog most evenings for nine years by a hill farmer with no one else to try it on. The dog did not have the joke. The dog had the last two seconds of it: the man's own laugh going off like a dropped pan, a hand coming down heavy on its head, then supper. That is a complete world, if you are a dog.

loreStory.t: Then the farmer's turn came, and the dog's came after, and the dog
woke in the meadow grass

like everything else that arrives here. It waited. He was not there, and he was not there the next season, and past a certain point the word for a man like that is the heaviest one in the language: he is one of the unwoken.

loreStory: A dog cannot draw a conclusion from that. It is the only mercy in the business.

So it waits at the head of any track that climbs toward a farm — hide gone patchy, ribs standing out, something green lifting off its spine in the cold — and through all of it the jaw has not slipped a hair, hung open and crooked and full of teeth, fixed in the two seconds before a hand comes down. People have tried feeding it. It is not hungry. It wants the two seconds.

monsters.name: Puddling
monsters.lore: A wobbling drop of pond water with a face. Cornered it bursts; beaten, it spreads out and quietly steams away.
monsters.loreDesc: Two big eyes in a wobble of pond water. Corner it and it bursts into spray, then gathers itself back up.
loreStory: No creature drowned to make the ponds' one. A low wet place got remembered by a great many people and visited by none of them, and the remembering pooled the way water pools, and one morning it had a face. Fight it and it bursts — alarming exactly once — sits a moment as a flat wet patch, and is a blob again before you have decided how you feel about that. Nothing lands. There is nothing in it to land on.

loreStory.t: The sorters' first question for any wild thing — what has it lost? — goes nowhere here, which is exactly why
Bettany

carried her whole list down to the pond and put every question to one aloud, in order, while it wobbled and watched her. It burst once, when a heron came down, and was back before she had finished the next question. Under its page in
the Chronicle
she wrote: stayed to the end of the questions, which is more than most people do. She maintains that this was an observation.
The pond, for what it is worth, has not moved since. Two Turns have been through the low country and left it exactly where her page says it is.
Gunnar
marks it on his maps as the stillest water in the district and, being Gunnar, will not say why he thinks so.

monsters.name: Snowmane
monsters.lore: White as the morning it vanished from the king's stable. It allows no rider, but walks beside the lost.
monsters.loreDesc: White as the morning it vanished from the king's stable. It allows no rider, but walks beside the lost.

loreStory.t: In life it was somebody's, and expensive, and one morning the stall stood empty with the door still bolted. That story is presumably still being told wrong in the living country. The truth is the ordinary one: it came the way everyone comes,
woke in the meadow grass
, and has no idea it is supposed to be a wonder.

loreStory: It will not be ridden and has never once made a fight of it. Put a saddle on and it stands patiently through the girth and the buckles; get a leg across and it simply walks out from under the whole arrangement and leaves you holding tack in an empty field. There is nothing there to argue with. Nothing was refused.

What it does instead is walk beside people who are lost — at the shoulder, at exactly their pace, for as long as it takes. Several have tried following it, on the reasonable assumption that a horse doing that must know a way, and been walked in a wide meandering circle back to their own footprints, because it was never leading. It goes where you go. All it does is see to it that a person alone in the dark is a person and a horse.

loreStory.t: Solveig

sees it more than anyone. Somebody comes stumbling in out of the dark towards the meadow fire with a white horse at their shoulder, and at the edge of the light the horse stops, and turns, and goes back out. It will not come in to the warm. The one courtesy she has never managed to do is thank it.

monsters.name: Fluffang
monsters.lore: Harmless-looking and quick to bolt, though the bite is real. A beginner's first honest mistake.
monsters.loreDesc: Tame in a way nothing wild is: it comes closer than it should, bolts, and bites in earnest when it cannot run.
loreStory: White is a poor colour in country that has things hunting in it, and the coat is not the strange part. The strange part is that it comes toward you. Nothing wild does that. A rabbit has decided in advance about every noise there is, and this one decides right about all of them, and then for a moment decides wrong: three or four steps in your direction, ears up, the way an animal moves toward a person it is expecting — then whatever is left inside catches up with it, and it is forty feet away. Somebody kept this one. The somebody got forgotten before the rabbit did.

loreStory.t: Twice a day it comes out onto the same patch of open ground within sight of
the meadow
, faces the same way, and waits. Nothing arrives.
Solveig

can see the spot from the fire, and when the fire can spare her she goes and sits at it — a little way off, at the hour, saying nothing. It will not take food from her; she is the wrong person, and it knows that better than it knows anything. She goes anyway. She has met strangers at their worst hour her whole watch, and she says a kept hour should not have to be kept alone.

loreStory: It will not turn while it still has somewhere to run. Take that away and it turns, and the teeth were always real. Most first seasons include this lesson, the gentlest on offer: nearly everything in this country will hurt you eventually, and almost none of it means to.

characters.name: Man
characters.lore: A young man of the human race — no claws, no scales, no magic in the blood, just nerve and a quick pair of hands. He sets out with nothing but what he stands in.
characters.loreDesc: Newly woken on the meadow with his name still on him, which is rarer than it sounds. What he was is over; what he will be has not been decided yet.

loreStory.t: He woke in the meadow grass with his name still on him, which is rarer than it sounds, and
Solveig

was beside him before the dew had soaked through his shirt. She told him the truth once, plainly, and asked his name and one true thing. The name came easily. The true thing took him until sundown — it was small, and she thanked him for it as if he had paid a debt, because here a true thing said aloud is exactly that.

loreStory: He still checks his pockets for something he last had on the other side. They are empty. So were everyone's — arriving with nothing is the one experience this whole country shares, and it is why a stranger here will feed you before you ask.

There is nothing remarkable about him, and this is not modesty: quick hands, a stubborn streak he had before the end, and no idea yet what either is for. Solveig is unworried. The ones who thank her, she says, always turn up at the meadow again sooner or later — on the far side of the courtesy, walking out into the wet grass to meet somebody new.

characters.name: Woman
characters.lore: A young woman of the human race, level-headed and hard to rattle. She carries no blade yet, only the stubborn confidence that carried humankind this far.
characters.loreDesc: Newly woken and hard to rattle. She had most of it worked out by the second evening, and has not yet said how she feels about any of it.
loreStory: She woke and took it better than most, which she is aware is a strange thing to be good at. By her second evening she had worked the rest out unassisted: that the fire was kindness rather than answers, and that the people being kind were not going to explain the important part, because they do not know it either. She has asked good questions ever since, and has not once asked whether it is really true.

loreStory.t: Bettany

came out from the stone house on her third morning, book open, the way she comes for everyone who will sit. The woman answered every question and then asked better ones back, which does not usually happen, and Bettany stayed past noon writing those down too. The last question, the gentle one — who she is waiting for — she was slowest to answer. What she said is not in the Chronicle; Bettany had already closed the book.

loreStory: What she is, is hard to rattle. Not brave the way the tellers mean it when they are working a room — brave in the flat, unremarkable way of somebody who looks at a thing that should be frightening, decides how frightened to be, and is then that frightened and no more. Everybody in this country is waiting for something. She has not said what. She will get around to it.

characters.name: Osric
characters.lore: Osric, a blacksmith of Nangijala. Hammer, apron, forge-burn up both arms. Judges a stranger by their edge.
characters.loreDesc: Blacksmith, newly woken, still counting in living years. He reads the meadow grass every morning before the forge is lit. His daughter turns nine this winter.

loreStory.t: The forge came before the grief could. He woke recently enough that the living country is still the country to him: he counts in living years, and will tell you mid-hammer that his daughter turns nine this winter —
the Human Dead

has that scene, and the loud hour that follows it. What it does not have is the shelf above his bench, where a ninth-winter gift already sits finished, months early, wrapped in oilcloth: a little iron horse with a mane he filed for a week, waiting on a delivery no smith can make.

He is waiting too. His wife went three winters ahead of him, and by his arithmetic she should have been standing in the meadow grass to meet him. So he walks the meadow's edge every morning before the forge is lit, and reads the grass, and comes back, and works.
The Waking

is honest about arithmetic like his. Twice now somebody at the fire has begun the sentence — some of the dead never — and both times the hammer came down on iron that did not need it. The sentence has stayed unfinished in his presence ever since, and people let him have that. Winter is long.
Sigrun

is taking the living words off him one at a time — he calls her the best teacher he never asked for — and she, who corrects everything, has left that sentence alone. Once, over the quenching trough, he asked her how long a person can decently wait. She let the steel stop singing first. As long as you keep the fire fed, she said. He took it for encouragement. It was not quite that.

characters.loreDesc: Weaponsmith. She hands every blade over hilt-first and watches how you take it — that is her deciding which of the trade's two words you are.

loreStory.t: What was left of her husband walked. A
Habit

shape runs one faithful loop, empty of anyone; his ran the roads he had walked home by all his life, and it ended at her door, and stood there, and did not knock. She let it stand the first time. By the third she understood what a shape on open road is to any stranger with a good eye and a day to spare. So she opened the door and let him finish arriving — all the way in, all the way home — and broke the shape herself, at the hearth, with the doors shut.
The hammer she uses now she made in the days between — a new head with a socket sunk in it, sized to a
stone

she did not yet hold. Practical people grieve forward. What rides in that socket is the trade's favourite story and not one she tells; what she will do is pass the finished blade across hilt-first and watch how it gets taken. Some people receive a sword. Some people take one. She has lifted a blade back out of a buyer's grip and returned the gold without explanation, and the trade has learned not to ask.
He says she is the best teacher he never asked for. She has heard him say it and let it stand, which from her is a great deal.
Osric

arrived weeks-woken with the living word for breaking things still in his mouth, and she took it off him inside a month — not by correcting him, but by making him watch her work until the wrong word embarrassed itself. He says she is the best teacher he never asked for, and she has let the sentence stand, which from her is a great deal. As for the name she has not said since that day at the hearth: it is not in this record, it is not in the Chronicle, and it is not going to be. She is not keeping it from anyone. She is keeping it.

characters.name: Solveig
characters.lore: Solveig, a townsfolk of Nangijala. One of Nangijala's own — no armour, no title, just a life being got on with.
characters.loreDesc: Keeper of the meadow fire, the first face the newly woken see. She finished a shift once that should have broken her, and has kept every one since.

loreStory.t: The watch was handed to her. She learned it from the woman before her — the seat with its back to the wind, the second cup in case a waking came thirsty, the courtesy word for word — and she loved her, in the unannounced way of a thousand shared quiet nights. One night, mid-vigil, mid-story — an old tale from the living country that Solveig had heard forty times and never once to the end, because something always interrupted — the voice went
Quiet

between one word and the next, and the bench was empty, and the fire wanted feeding. Solveig fed it. She kept the watch to sunrise and met the morning's waking with a level voice. Then she walked out past the woodpile and cried until the sun was high.
Her name was Tove. It is in
the Chronicle
because Solveig went to
Bettany

the week after and stood over the page until every letter was down. And she still tells the unfinished story at the fire, exactly as far as it goes, and asks everyone she meets there, once the shaking stops, whether they knew that tale in life. Somebody crossed over knowing the ending. One evening somebody will wake in that grass carrying it, and she means to be sitting there when they do.

loreStory: She could go on any evening — she is as whole as anyone left — and everyone knows what she says about staying: if she goes, who meets them? What she does not say is that Tove could have gone once too, and stayed for the same reason, and stayed past the going. Solveig stands in a door she watched close on the woman before her, and stands there anyway, on purpose. Ask how long she has kept the watch and you get the answer Tove used to give: since morning.

characters.name: Wendell
characters.lore: Wendell, a village elder of Nangijala. Old enough to remember the last bad winter and mean it as a warning.
characters.loreDesc: Elder of the meadow fire. He pays for company with the east road, one evening at a time, and knows better than anyone how much road he has left.

loreStory.t: The oldest head at the meadow fire pays his way in road. What he sells — the carts, the inn at the ford, the summer the verge came up in flowers — and where he walks when the weather is quiet, and beside whom, is told in
the Quiet

, and told right. What that chapter is too kind to add: a telling keeps the east road firm under feet that still walk it, so every evening he sells is maintenance, and every listener who thinks they are indulging an old man is holding up a road without knowing whose.

Last winter he caught himself putting the flowers in the wrong summer. A small slip, the kind any teller makes — except that everyone who could have corrected him is gone, and the road is now exactly as true as his remembering, no truer. He finished the story, said nothing, and began a private tally that night: which stretch, sold to whom, how often, what he no longer trusts.
Bettany
has the whole road saved, forty pages, milestone by milestone; for her evenings he trades a different memory altogether, a thread a week, and knows exactly what he is doing.

loreStory: Ask why a man that old and that whole has never gone on, and you will be paid in road stories. The true answer walks a fixed stretch at a fixed hour and holds only while somebody keeps saying carts, ford, flowers. He does not name her, and neither will this book. He is running out of road and running out of evenings, and he has already decided, telling no one, which of the two of them gets the last of it.

characters.name: Hearn
characters.lore: Hearn, a grizzled veteran of Nangijala. Too old for the front rank, too stubborn to say so. Carries knives where the young carry hope.
characters.loreDesc: Veteran of the one attempt anyone made on the cave. He came back alone, buys rounds for those who did not, and says only that it asked politely.

loreStory.t: What the whole country knows about him fits in
one chapter

: the summer morning, the best the fires had, the evening he came back out alone, unhollowed, unmarked, and the three words every asker since has been paid. This record will not improve on it. What it can add is the shape of his evenings. He buys rounds for people who are not there to drink them, and the ritual has an order: the same cups, the same places at the table, filled and left standing, and his own drunk last, facing the door.
People read the silence as a wound and grant it the wide berth wounds get.
Bettany

tested it. She asked him nothing about the inside — only about the ones who went in — and he talked until the candles were done: names, trades, who owed whom, who sang badly on the walk east, freely and warmly and in order. His account of that morning is the fullest thing in
the Chronicle
, and it stops at the mouth of the cave like a cut rope. A wound does not choose its edges that cleanly. A promise does.
What was promised, and to whom, is nowhere in this book, because he has kept it out of every book, and pays for the keeping in public and in small change: the rounds he cannot afford, the
eastern stone

sold under its price the same evening it was paid to him, the seat that faces the door. He could go on — he is as whole as the day he walked out, which is its own uncomfortable fact — and he stays, and keeps the cups filled, and lets everyone call it grief, because the truth has no polite shape: silence that is kept was silence given to someone, and Hearn is good for his debts.

characters.name: Gunnar
characters.pixellabName: I want you to only c (copy 5)
characters.lore: Gunnar, a road-worn wanderer of Nangijala. Grey cloak, plain sword, no home worth naming. Passing through, as always.
characters.loreDesc: Wanderer. He maps the Drift with stakes and string, walks the eastern line every year, and has stopped telling anybody what the measurements say.
loreStory: Most people meet a Turn the morning after, when the path goes somewhere new. Gunnar meets it in the numbers. He walks the country with stakes and knotted string and a ledger of small tidy figures, re-measuring what everyone else re-remembers, and for years he did it out loud — sheets posted at the fires, a hamlet warned its ford was going, the shore people told which cliff not to build under. They thanked him and built there anyway, or moved and grumbled, and either way the maps did what maps are for.

loreStory.t: Then his eastern line began coming back wrong in one direction only. Soft ground — the kind that forgets faster than anyone is forgetting it — moving year on year, not wandering the way the Drift wanders but travelling, and travelling toward the meadow.
The Hole Under the Mountain
says he has stopped telling anybody what he measures, and it is so. The spring he was sure, he walked to the meadow fire, sat down across from
Solveig
, accepted the second cup, and talked for an hour about the weather. Then he thanked her and left. He has made that walk three springs running.

loreStory: His reasoning is as tidy as the ledger: a fright helps no one who cannot act on it; the fires cannot move a meadow; so the knowing should sit with the one man fit to carry it. That is also why he has never gone on — you cannot leave, he says, in the middle of a measurement. The flaw in the reasoning is not on his maps. It is in the man: he has mistaken carrying a thing alone for keeping people safe from it, and the ground is not slowing down.

characters.name: Jehanne
characters.lore: Jehanne, a priestess of Nangijala. Keeps the quiet rites nobody watches. Kind, and entirely unbudgeable.
characters.loreDesc: Priestess of a faith she no longer believes and cannot stop practising. Ask her and she will say so. Watch her hold a service and you will not believe her.

loreStory.t: The believing fell out of her somewhere on the crossing, and she will say so to anyone who asks, flat as a floorboard. Why she holds the services anyway is in
the Human Dead

, and it is the truth: the practice is a rota by another name, the candles are a fire, people come and stay and talk, and the talk is the thing. All of that she will admit in daylight. What she will not admit is what happens to her voice inside the service.

Ask her at the woodpile and the prayer goes to no one; ask her mid-liturgy and you would swear she had seen the answer. She never decided on the lie. It arrived like a work-skill, the way a smith's arm learns the blow: the old words want certainty behind them, and her body supplies it, and forty faces steady in the candlelight because the priest is sure. Last spring she sat with a friend at
Faded

— a woman losing the faces of her own children — who asked the bare question: will I be held? Jehanne heard her own voice say yes, whole and warm, not a splinter of doubt in it, and watched the woman settle under the word. It bought her a season. Jehanne walked home in the dark, was sick at the crossroads, and has never told anyone which part of the evening did that.

loreStory: She could go on; she is remembered whole by half the fireside, which is more than most can claim. She stays because the rota is short-handed, she says, and it is true, and it is not the reason. The reason is the forty faces. They believe her certainty, not her confession — and if she left, the leaving would tell them which one was real.

characters.name: Bettany
characters.pixellabName: I want you to only c (copy 3)
characters.lore: Bettany, a scribe of Nangijala. Keeps ledgers nobody reads until the day everybody does.
characters.loreDesc: Scribe of the Chronicle — the book in your hands. She began it the day her grief went missing, and she will not close it until she knows what took it.

loreStory.t: Britt was the younger by six years and the quicker by every measure that is fun at a fair, and the sisters sang in parts — Britt above, Bettany under — through every wash-day of two lifetimes, the living one and this one. What happened when Britt went on is told in
the Long Morning
, and Bettany would rather you read it there. The short of it: everyone the going-on bereaves loses the grief itself, and everyone but her has agreed to call that mercy.
In the back of
the Chronicle

, past the last written page, there is a private column of dates. On Britt's day each year Bettany sings both parts of the wash-song alone, her line and then her sister's — she has lost none of it, which is the whole horror — and waits to feel anything at all, and writes the result beside the date. The column is longer now than some chapters. Every entry says: still nothing. She is a careful scribe. If it ever says something else, she wants to know the day.
She interviews everyone who will sit, and most sit once.
Wendell

gets her a whole evening every week and believes it is for his east road, which she has duly saved — forty pages, milestone by milestone. She keeps coming for a different reason. Wendell met Britt once, at a shearing, and he tells it a little differently each time — the dress, the weather, what Britt called across the pen — and Bettany sits very still through every version, waiting for the one with something new in it. He knows exactly what he is doing. He spins that morning out a thread a week, because the evenings are what he is really trading for; she pays, and both of them let the price go on being called the road.

objects.loreDesc: A stain is a story that ended at the nearest fire. Almost always.
loreStory: Fights end. The broken go down where they stand and, some hours on, stand up again beside the nearest tended fire, short a little of whatever they were thinking when it happened. That is the arithmetic of violence here: it costs a thought, not a life. So a stain on the stones is not a marker. It is the start of a story that finished somewhere warmer — an argument gone too far, a robbery on the road, a creature that had to be released the hard way — and by the time the rain gets around to it, the person it came out of has usually walked past it twice without looking down.

loreStory.t: Usually. The re-forming needs a tended fire, and the rota has lapsed almost everywhere. Out where the map has gone
Quiet
, the nearest fire can be a long way to nowhere. The old hands read stains the way trackers read prints: fresh means a scuffle. Faded, far from any light, means don't ask.

objects.loreDesc: The fire on the meadow. It has never once been let go out.

loreStory.t: It has never gone out. That is not a figure of speech: it is the fire Signe lit, or a fire fed from it, or a fire people only say was fed from it, and in this country all three are the same wood. Every soul that ever opened its eyes on the meadow saw this light first — before the stone house, before the grass, before their own name came back to them.
The waking
is cold and confused everywhere except within reach of it.
Solveig

keeps it now. There is a seat with its back to the wind, a second cup in case the newest arrival comes thirsty, and split wood stacked like a promise. When she asks your name and one true thing, look into the flames while you answer; everyone does. What is said there holds.

loreStory: Feed it if you pass. Not because it needs you tonight — because one night it will, and it does not announce which.

objects.loreDesc: A cross over no grave, raised for someone who never woke.
loreStory: Nothing is buried under it. Nothing is ever buried here: the Quiet leaves no body, no bone, no weight for a shovel. A grave is a living country's answer to a problem this one does not have.

loreStory.t: The crosses are for the other absence. People die together — a sickness, a wreck, a winter — and one of them wakes on the meadow and the other never comes.
The waking

owes no explanation and gives none. So the woken do the one thing left to do: they cut two pieces of wood, plant them where the missing one would have been welcome, and say the name aloud, on the old understanding that what is spoken holds. It is the only telling in Nangijala that does not work. The name holds nothing, because the person it belongs to is not here to be held. They say it anyway. Every cross on the map is somebody still saying it.

items.name: Abalone
items.description: Half a shell lined in green and gold fire. Dunedelver turns them up from a sea that dried out long ago.
items.loreDesc: Half a shell lined in green and gold fire. Dunedelver turns them up from a sea that dried out long ago.
loreStory: The inside of one does the northern sky when a fire catches it: green sheeting into gold, then gone, then back a little to the left. People notice. People have always noticed, and the dune camps have priced accordingly.

loreStory.t: Who buys them is the part worth writing down. It is the ones left behind by
the Long Morning

— the sister, the man whose friend of four hundred years was simply not in the room one evening — and they are not fooled, and will say so before you can raise it. It is a shell. It is not that light. They buy it anyway and set it where they will catch it by accident, on a sill, beside a door, because a thing that ambushes you with that colour twice a week is as near as they can get to being reminded of somebody they cannot manage to miss.

items.name: Amber Root
items.description: Hacked off a Stumpling's root-leg and glazed hard with amber sap. Warm to hold, and alchemists know it.
items.loreDesc: Hacked off a Stumpling's root-leg and glazed hard in amber sap. Warm in the hand, and it holds a fire till morning.
loreStory: It is no good for burning bright. Set one in the ash under the real wood and it sulks along all night, and at fourth watch, when the rest of the hearth has gone grey, there is still a red eye in there and a keeper who has had two hours lying down. That is what thirty-four gold buys. Not warmth, not light. Two hours.

loreStory.t: There are four in a crate under the table in
the hall on the meadow
Solveig

did not buy them, will not ask who did, and has never said out loud that she needs them. They turn up, one or two at a time, at the start of the cold. Somebody on that road is spending real money to see that the woman who meets the wakings gets to lie down, and has never put a name to it or stayed for a cup.

items.name: Amethyst
items.description: A single violet point, flat-faced and flawless. Amethyrn grazes on these and swallows the ones it likes.
items.loreDesc: A single violet point, flat-faced and flawless. Amethyrn grazes on these and swallows the ones it likes.

loreStory.t: You do not mine these. You follow.
Amethyrn

eats what it likes and passes what it does not, and a man walking a day behind a feeding bull can make a season off the road without swinging at anything. The flat faces are why the trade pays over the odds: a grazed point comes up already tabled, and a cutter who has not had to cut charges as though he had. There is a follower on the north fells who has kept to one bull for eleven years. He knows its temper, its slow circuit, where it beds. He stopped calling it prospecting a while ago. Asked what he calls it now, he said the bull was easier company than a fire, because a fire wants you to talk.

items.name: Hawk Feather
items.description: Barred brown with an olive tip, and too big for any bird anyone has flushed out of these woods yet.
items.loreDesc: Barred brown with an olive tip, and too big for any bird anyone has flushed out of these woods yet.

loreStory.t: There are no hawks. A stall cannot sell large brown feather, source unknown, so a man in the second row called it a hawk feather about forty years ago and it has been a hawk feather ever since — every stall, every sack, seven gold. He sells a
Hawk Quill

as well, off nothing anyone has seen either. The joke wore out a long time ago. He believes in the hawk now, entirely and with heat, and will describe it to you at length, and the description is the same every time.

items.name: Hawk Quill
items.description: A stiff barred quill, blue at the base. Fletchers would pay if anyone could say what it came off.
items.loreDesc: A stiff barred quill, blue at the base. Fletchers would pay if anyone could say what it came off.

loreStory.t: A fletcher wants three off one wing: same curve, same stiffness, same hand of twist, or the arrow walks. These come up singly, out of sacks, off different somethings, and no two of them match — which is why a quill good enough for war is worth eight gold and a matched three would be worth forty.
Sigrun
will fletch to order and will not buy singles, and says so before you have the bag open. The carts take them anyway, by weight, unmatched, at the same price they pay for twigs.

items.name: Obsidian
items.description: Fist-sized lump of glossy black glass, cooled out of some fire-thing's crust. Keen enough to shave with, so don't.
items.loreDesc: Fist-sized lump of glossy black glass, cooled out of some fire-thing's crust. Keen enough to shave with, so don't.
loreStory: Knapped into flakes it gives the finest edge in the trade and survives about four minutes of work. Steel drags; glass parts. When you are opening a broken shape for what sits at the bottom of it, drag is what scars a stone, and a scarred stone loses a third of its price — so the careful carry a lump and strike a fresh flake off it as they go, using each until it dulls and dropping it where they kneel.

loreStory.t: Which means a working site glitters. Come up a hillside at low sun and you can read exactly where somebody stopped, how long they took over it, and from the count of flakes how much trouble the shape gave them.
Cracking
is a private profession that leaves the tidiest record of itself of any work in Nangijala, and the trade has never managed to break the habit.

items.name: Black Glass
items.description: Slab of black volcanic glass, faceted and chipped. It sheds off a Magmashell's plates as the fire cools.
items.loreDesc: Slab of black volcanic glass, faceted and chipped. It sheds off a Magmashell's plates as the fire cools.
loreStory: Ground flat and worked with wet sand for a week, a slab this size is a mirror, and a dark one — it takes about a third of the light out of whatever it shows you. The trade knows to sell them outdoors at noon. Indoors by a candle, everyone looks like the end of a long year.

loreStory.t: The buyers are mostly old, and there is a use for a mirror in a country where
the stages

are only ever learned from outside: you look, daily, and you check that the face doing the looking is one you can still put a name to. An elder on the east road bought a slab, brought it back the following morning and asked for his money. The seller said the glass was accurate. The elder said yes, that was the complaint.

items.name: Dark Horns
items.description: A pair of black horns tipped in sickly green. Thornstag drops one every autumn and grows it back worse.
items.loreDesc: A pair of black horns tipped in sickly green. Thornstag drops one every autumn and grows it back worse.

loreStory.t: Out east the year is not counted, it is picked up.
Thornstag

sheds one horn every autumn within a night or two of the same night, and a household on that road has been gathering them since before anyone there can date, one to a shelf, in order, the oldest by the door. Thirty-four gold apiece if they ever sold one. They never have, because the shelf is the only almanac that stretch of country has, and people will walk a day and a half to stand in the doorway and count back to the autumn they are trying to place.

loreStory: Count the other way and you get the thing they do not walk there for. The green is climbing. On the ones by the door it is a fleck at the point. On this year's it is a third of the way up the horn.

items.name: Onyx Shard
items.description: Wedge of near-black glass with a cold blue sheen, cracked out of Rimeshard's rock. The edge never dulls.
items.loreDesc: Wedge of near-black glass with a cold blue sheen, cracked out of Rimeshard's rock. The edge never dulls.
loreStory: The edge never dulls, so nobody sharpens one, so a man who owns one has nothing to do with his hands of an evening and does it anyway.

loreStory.t: Hearn
carries a shard off a
Rimeshard

on the black rock, in a sleeve on his belt, and has not cut anything with it since he came back down the mountain on his own. After the fire is banked he takes it out, wipes it on his knee, holds it up, turns it, puts it away. Every night. Someone at his fire made a joke of it once. He waited for the laugh to finish and said it was not for the mountain, it was for the walk home, and did not say which walk.

items.name: Rib Cage
items.description: Spine and curved ribs, bleached clean. A Palehusk wore it badly, and a Glowbone would have lit it up.
items.loreDesc: Spine and curved ribs, bleached clean. A Palehusk wore it badly, and a Glowbone would have lit it up.
loreStory: Sold by the cage, priced by the rib, and that is where the trade does its small daily cheating. A rib is the best stock going for anything long and slightly bent — netting needles, comb teeth, a splint to bind a cracked shaft — and the flat of a big one makes a better knife scale than any wood. So count them at the counter. The seller counts thirteen a side out of habit, the buyer counts what is actually there, and the gap between those two numbers has bought a great deal of drink on that road.

loreStory.t: Osric

counted one out loud, all the way to the end, in front of the man selling it. He was advised, evenly and by everyone present at once, never to do that again. He still does not entirely see why, and the road has decided that is the best thing about him.

items.name: Sea Shells
items.description: Scallops and spirals, sun-faded to tan. A Dunedelver turns them up where the sea has not been for an age.
items.loreDesc: Scallops and spirals, sun-faded to tan. A Dunedelver turns them up where the sea has not been for an age.

loreStory.t: Eleven gold a handful — on the dune road, at the crossings, from anybody, in any season. That figure has not moved in anyone's memory, which makes sea shells the steadiest price in the world after
gold itself

, and the trade uses them as a ruler: when two people cannot agree what a hide is worth, one of them says it in handfuls and the argument is finished inside a minute. The reason is not flattering. Prices move because people want things, and want is the unsteady part, and nothing about a scallop faded to the colour of a fingernail has ever moved anybody. The trade got its one honest measure out of the only goods in the country nobody has ever wanted.

items.name: Glow Caps
items.description: Blue mushrooms on a knot of root, lit from inside. Gnarloak carries a whole grove in its shoulders.
items.loreDesc: Blue mushrooms on a knot of root, lit from inside. Gnarloak carries a whole grove in its shoulders.

loreStory.t: It does not go out. Not for wind, not for rain, not for a ford — a knot of root with nine or ten caps burns dim and blue and cold in the hand for four months, and costs thirty gold.
Gunnar
walks nights with one caged in wire on his pack and considers the matter settled.
Wendell

will not have one in the house, and puts it plainly. A lamp lets you keep walking. A fire makes you stop, and sit, and put your hands out, and then somebody says a true thing and somebody else is there to hear it. He knows how that sounds coming from an old man. He is an old man. He has also spent forty years selling one road at a fireside, a listening at a time, to keep it firm under somebody's feet, and he does not bring her into the argument. Gunnar, who knows about her, does not either.

items.name: Blue Scales
items.description: A sheet of blue-green scales, cold and slick. Nothing in this valley wears a coat quite like it.
items.loreDesc: A sheet of blue-green scales, cold and slick. Nothing in this valley wears a coat quite like it.

loreStory.t: Hold a piece in a closed fist as long as you can stand it and it will still be cold when you let go, and so will your hand, for an hour after.
Osric

has a strip stitched into the back of his left glove — the hand that holds the work, not the hammer — and it has bought him a few more seconds at the anvil every day for two years. That is not why he bought it. He bought it because a man three years dead can set this stuff on a bench, come back in the morning, and find it behaving exactly as it did the morning before, which is more than the grass outside the forge will do for him. The gold along one edge is where the blue stopped and something else began. The strip will not say what.

items.name: Rift Geode
items.description: Split grey stone bleeding cold cyan light from every seam. Golems grow around them and resent the loss.
items.loreDesc: Split grey stone bleeding cold cyan light from every seam. Golems grow around them and resent the loss.
loreStory: They arrive split. You do not open one; you find it open, lit from a hollow in the middle by a cold cyan that has no source you can point at and does not go out when you cover it.

loreStory.t: There is a standing order on them, older than anyone now working
the sheds

: every geode bought, sight unseen, a hundred and sixty in gold, the same price for a fist and for one you need both arms under. Nobody buys stone that way. Stone goes by weight and grade, and this buyer has never asked after either, never haggled, never said what they are for. The crews stopped asking; the money is good and the questions are unpaid. A man at the east weighing-post tried a fake last spring — grey rubble, a hollow cut with a lamp, coloured glass. It was bought. Same price, no comment. He tells it now as a joke. He has also stopped going to the weighing-post himself.

items.name: Beast Tooth
items.description: Thumb-long ivory with a notched crown. A Palemaw bites once; a Diretusk never has to. Both leave these.
items.loreDesc: Thumb-long ivory with a notched crown. A Palemaw bites once; a Diretusk never has to. Both leave these.

loreStory.t: Gold

does not divide small enough. Everybody here agrees about gold, which is precisely the trouble: the smallest coin anybody will cut is still worth more than a night's guiding, an hour of somebody's back, or a bed by a fire in weather. So below gold the road runs on teeth.

loreStory: An ivory of this grade is the unit. Eighteen gold nominal; in practice one favour, and every fire on that road knows the size of a favour without anyone having to set it down. You leave one under the flat stone at a crossing when you owe and cannot stop to pay. There is a crossing on the east road with four under the stone, all of them gone grey. Whoever left them has been back past. Whoever they were for has not.

items.name: Bog Slime
items.description: Swamp-green and faintly gritty, with things suspended in it you would rather not name.
items.loreDesc: Swamp-green and faintly gritty, with things suspended in it you would rather not name.

loreStory.t: The grit is why anyone buys it. Every glob out of a crossing is a squeeze of that crossing's bottom, so the fen stalls press each one flat between two boards before it goes in the jar, on the strength of what has come out over the years: teeth, buttons, fish-hooks, a brass hinge, coins from four centuries in one afternoon, and once a walker's ring out of a shallow
the frog
has held since before the roads were where they are.

loreStory: A woman comes to that market and asks to do the pressing herself. She buys none of it. She lost something at a ford a long time ago and can no longer say what it was, only that her hands will know it when they find it. Everyone lets her press. She is Bright by every measure the trade has, she has been coming for four years, and the stall keeps her boards behind the counter.

items.name: Grave Dirt
items.description: Crumbly dark earth studded with bone chips. Whatever the Palehusk climbed out of, it brought some along.
items.loreDesc: Crumbly dark earth studded with bone chips, out of a Palehusk's creases. Field soil — and nothing is farmed up there.
loreStory: Five gold the bag, the cheapest thing anyone carries down off the black rock, and it sells at all because of one woman at the sorting sheds. She farmed, in life. She can put a district to a handful of dirt the way other people put a face to a name — rubs it, smells it, gives you a valley — and the carters have checked her twice against ground they knew, and she was right twice.

loreStory.t: Everything she has been handed out of
the pale ones

is field soil. Ploughed loam, with the bone chips of somebody's stock crushed through it. Nothing is farmed on the black rock and nothing ever was, so the things came up from somewhere on foot, carrying a farm in their creases the whole way. The sheds keep the bags by district now and send the list down to
the Chronicle
each season. She has named nineteen valleys. Not one of them has been hers.

items.name: Root Bundle
items.description: Brown roots tied off with twine and dried brittle. Whatever woodland lump was hauling it does not want it back.
items.loreDesc: Thin roots bound in twine and dried past bending. Sold in autumn, to go into the ground in spring.
loreStory: A woman on the north road digs, trims, ties and dries them, forty bundles a season, and sells them off a board at the autumn markets to anyone with a bed to fill. Most of it is trade. One order is not.

loreStory.t: The same order every year, placed in advance, in the same hand: white bellflower, two bundles, held back until the frost breaks.
Jehanne

has never said whether they took. The digger has never asked, and has settled it privately, and will tell you so over a cup — that the ground behind that chapel must be a sight by now, white to the wall, thick as a hedge, coming again every spring for eleven years. She has not gone to look. She has eleven years of the same order in her book in the same hand, which she says is a better thing to own than a garden.

items.name: Old Compass
items.description: Brass, scratched, and still pointing true. Its owner is somewhere in Palehusk's collection of skins.
items.loreDesc: Brass, scratched, and still pointing true. In a country that rearranges itself, that is less useful than it sounds.

loreStory.t: It came off the black rock, prised out of a
Palehusk

's fingers, needle still swinging clean, which is more than can be said for whatever it was doing out there. The country it was bought for is somewhere else now. The needle does not care. It swings, settles, points north — and north here is the one direction with an opinion already attached, being where the winter sky goes green. What a person makes of that is their own business. The compass makes nothing of it.
Gunnar

pays sixty-five gold, over the odds, and he is not buying a way to find anything. Two fixed marks and a good needle will tell you how far a piece of ground has turned since the last time you stood on it. He has a drawer of compasses and a book of figures, and he will gladly show you the compasses. There is a page in the book with the meadow on it. He has shown that page to nobody.

items.name: Plume Bundle
items.description: Green, teal, blue and red plumes lashed to a cord. Nothing in these woods wears feathers like that.
items.loreDesc: Green, teal, blue and red plumes lashed to a cord. Nothing in these woods wears feathers like that.

loreStory.t: Four ordinary plumes lashed together sell for more than four ordinary plumes. Every stall knows it, every stall does it, and the seller's knot is a flat two-turn hitch you can spot from across a market. This one is tied with a bootlace, badly, twice over. Bundles like that were not made to be sold. They were made to be given, by somebody with no gold who wanted to put something into a hand, and they reach a stall when the giving does not happen.
Solveig
buys those ones at the asking price, does not haggle, and has a box.

items.name: Broken Tusk
items.description: Snapped off at the root, cream shading to brown. The Diretusk it belonged to never broke stride.
items.loreDesc: Snapped off at the root, cream shading to brown. The Diretusk it belonged to never broke stride.

loreStory.t: A whole tusk fetches four times what a broken one does, and there is a man on the north market road who makes up the difference with bone glue, a lathe and thirty years of practice. The join sits under the curve, where a buyer's thumb never goes. He has sold mended tusks to people who have handled tusks their whole span, and one of them was
Sigrun
, who spotted it at the door on her way out, went back in, and bought a second one to work out how he had done it.

loreStory: She has never said a word about him to anyone on that road. He is also the only buyer at that market who pays a new cracker the real price for a first bag rather than what a frightened person will take. Everybody there knows both halves of this. The market runs on it, cheerfully, and has for years.

items.name: Bronze Knife
items.description: Camp bronze on a ribbed wooden grip, made for rope and rations. The Nightmule that hauled it went feral first.
items.loreDesc: Camp bronze on a ribbed wooden grip, made for rope and rations. It comes off a mule that is carrying nothing.

loreStory.t: It is sold as a trophy and it is a bread knife. Soft bronze, the edge honed back three fingers' worth over years, a guard on it because guards were the fashion where it was made and not because anything was ever coming the other way.
Sigrun
has had a dozen of them across her bench and says the same thing about every one: this has never been fought with. It cut rope. It cut rations. It went back in the roll clean.
Buyers hear that and pay the thirty-two gold anyway, because a knife that came down off
an animal still walking the old east road

is a story and a bread knife is not. Sigrun does not argue them out of it. Her view is that they have the better story and have picked the wrong reason for wanting it — somebody packed this for a journey, with cheese and a length of rope, and the journey is still going.

items.name: Bronze Cog
items.description: A toothed bronze wheel, still greased. Runemane is full of these, and one of them is why it still runs.
items.loreDesc: A toothed bronze wheel, still greased and still turning easily. There is nothing left anywhere to fit it into.

loreStory.t: Twenty-eight gold, and worth it as a curiosity and nothing else. The hall it turned in went. The
lion at the door
did not, and
Wendell
walked that road while the roof was still on and will give you the animal in detail and not one single thing about the room behind it.

loreStory: The cogs came through too, and by the hundred, and looking at one tells you why. A toothed wheel is about as little as a made thing can be. You can hold the whole of it in your head at a glance, and hand it to somebody else in one sentence, and no two people out of two different centuries would describe it any differently. A hall full of machinery is not like that. So what survives of a building nobody can name is the parts of it that fit in a hand — still greased, still turning sweetly, geared to each other and to nothing at all.

items.name: Grain Sack
items.description: A burlap sack of oats, gnawed open at one corner. Sorrel has been carrying its own feed for years.
items.loreDesc: A burlap sack of oats, gnawed open at one corner. Sorrel has been carrying its own feed for years.

loreStory.t: The oats are worth nothing and wet sacking less. What sells is the corner, where a farm's mark is stitched into the weave — three lines and a hook, so the mill gives you back your own sacks and not somebody else's. A collector cut that corner out and carried it round the fires, asking.
Wendell

could not place it, and was short with people for a week afterwards. Four fires on, a man set his cup down and said that is my father's mark, we had it on the sacks and the gate and the churn — and then sat holding it, and could not produce his father's name, and the fire waited the way fires do. He bought the corner. He paid gold for a corner of sacking. Everyone there thought it was cheap.

items.name: Wood Idol
items.description: A squat figure carved from dark wood, worn faceless by handling. Runemane's temple is full of them.
items.loreDesc: A squat figure of dark wood, arms folded, eyes shut, rubbed to a shine. They come up out of the grass by the dozen.

loreStory.t: The trade calls them idols because it needs a word. Nobody has produced a name for the figure, a rite it belonged to, or one person who ever knelt to one, and that is not for want of asking — they come up in the grass by the dozen where
Runemane
walks its round, and the only plan of the building is a sheet of
Gunnar
's with nothing to write at the top of it.
They brought one to
Jehanne

, on the reasonable grounds that she is the nearest thing to an expert this road has. She turned it over twice — the shine on them is thumbs, and there are a very great many thumbs in that shine — said she had never seen the like, gave it back, and went out to keep her evening rota. She kept the second one. It sits on the shelf over her table, arms folded, eyes shut, seventy gold any day she wanted seventy gold, and she has stopped explaining to people why it is there.

items.name: Dew Drop
items.description: A drop of water that will not evaporate or spill. Dewling wears one like a crown and guards it badly.
items.loreDesc: A drop of water that will not evaporate or spill. Dewling wears one like a crown and guards it badly.

loreStory.t: A drop that keeps its curve keeps it exactly, so what you get looking through one at arm's length is the far side of the valley, small and bright and upside down. Cutlers use them to check an edge.
Gunnar

uses his to read his own far stakes without walking to them, which takes the eastern line from three days down to one. He buys at the wet-field stall, eighteen gold, off whatever the crackers bring in from the
Dewlings

, and he buys one a year, every year, because the neck clouds over by autumn and he will not measure through a clouded one. The stallholder keeps the tally out of politeness and has never once been asked for it. Last spring he came back inside the same season and bought a second.

items.name: Clear Wing
items.description: A single glassy wing, veined like a leaf. Whatever hatched it is bigger than anything you want to meet.
items.loreDesc: A single glassy wing, veined like a leaf. Whatever hatched it is bigger than anything you want to meet.

loreStory.t: Oiled and set in a frame it makes the cheapest window in the country and a better one than glass: it will not yellow, it will not craze, and it takes a knock. Half the lanterns on the east road are looking out through one. It is not an
Emberwing
's — those are scaled, and they burn. Every lantern-maker on that road can give you the span of the animal to the inch, off the taper of the veins, and not one of them has laid eyes on it.

items.name: Quartz Shard
items.description: Prised out of Mosscairn rubble and Rimeshard ice alike: one six-sided white point ringed with chippings.
items.loreDesc: Prised out of Mosscairn rubble and Rimeshard ice alike: one six-sided white point ringed with chippings.
loreStory: Quartz is the don't-know bin. Everything else on the sorting bench announces where it came from — a tooth is a jaw, a hide is a back, a green crust is a road somebody can name — and quartz comes off five different creatures identically, so the moment it is off the animal it is off the record.

loreStory.t: Which is why apprentices are set to sell it. There is no price to ruin. What they are actually being taught, over a year of being told no, is the thing that runs
the whole trade

: people are not buying stone, they are buying the story fastened to it, and a white six-sided point with no story attached is the hardest sale in the sheds. The day one of them manages it, the master buys the drink.

items.name: Ice Cluster
items.description: A crown of clear ice spires on a frozen base. It does not melt, and it does not like being held.
items.loreDesc: A crown of clear ice spires on a frozen base. It does not melt, and it does not like being held.
loreStory: Bare hands stick to it and come away short, so it travels in straw like an egg and every buyer is warned twice. A third of them try it anyway.

loreStory.t: Most go to people who cannot sleep warm. There is a woman two fires east who keeps one under her cot and the shutter open in every season, and she has been asked, kindly, whether that is not a hard way to live. She says the cold was the last thing she felt on the other side and the first thing she lost in
the grass
, and that a person is allowed one souvenir. Then she asks you to shut the door on your way out, from the outside.

items.name: Stone Egg
items.description: Fitted stone plates packed into an oval, shaken loose from a Magmashell. Nothing has ever hatched out of one.
items.loreDesc: Fitted stone plates packed into an oval, shaken loose from a Magmashell. Nothing has ever hatched out of one.

loreStory.t: They sell best within sight of
the meadow

, and the sellers know exactly why. Someone three days woken cannot give you their name yet but can already feel the shape of the problem, which is that in this country everything has happened already. An egg is the only thing on the stall that points the other way.

loreStory: The stallholders do not lie about it. Ask outright and you will be told: no, nothing comes out, it is stone through and through, they have sawn one open. They still sell four a week. A woman on the south path has kept hers eleven years, in the ash at the edge of her hearth, turned twice a day, and when this is put to her as foolishness she agrees that it is, and turns it, and says that having a thing to do at the same hour every day is not nothing.

items.name: Bog Worm
items.description: A fat pink worm, still coiling slowly. Mirewart eats them by the dozen and leaves the tough ones.
items.loreDesc: A fat pink worm, still coiling slowly. Mirewart eats them by the dozen and leaves the tough ones.

loreStory.t: It is the only thing on a junk stall that moves, so it is kept in a tin and sold the same day. Bait, mostly. But the fen-walkers buy them for the reading: what
the frog

passes over is what has been in that water longest, so a fat tough one out of a shallow means the shallow has been a shallow for years and will still be there when you come back. A crossing full of thin new worms is a crossing that was somewhere else last season. Cross it early, and cross it once.

items.name: Coiled Rope
items.description: Braided tan hemp, chewed to a splay at one end by a Nightmule with opinions. Still holds a knot, mostly.
items.loreDesc: Braided tan hemp, chewed to a splay at one end by a Nightmule with opinions. Still holds a knot, mostly.

loreStory.t: Gunnar

buys rope. Any rope, any length, over the odds, and a chewed end does not put him off — he ties the chewed end, so the good end takes the weight. A cracker who was certain he was being made a fool of followed him east one autumn to find out what a man wants with forty lengths of hemp. He found him at a gorge crossing, hanging a new line twenty feet along from an old line that ended in air. The far anchor had gone with the ground it was in. Gunnar measured the gap, wrote it in the ledger, finished the knot, and said nothing about any of it at any fire that season. Eight gold is what the rope is worth. The arithmetic is what he is paying for.

items.name: Rope Lasso
items.description: A stiff coil of rope with a running loop, chewed through near the knot. Sorrel got loose years ago.
items.loreDesc: A stiff coil of rope with a running loop, chewed through near the knot. Sorrel got loose years ago.

loreStory.t: The courtesy asks a newly woken soul for two things: a name, and one true thing. A man came up out of the meadow grass one spring with neither. He sat where
Solveig

put him, took the second cup, could not say what he was called or where he had been, and then saw the coil by the woodpile and asked for it with a look. He made the loop up the way other people tie a shoe. Then he put it over the corner post of the woodshed at eleven paces, four times running, and sat down on the bench and cried, and was still nameless in the morning. Solveig wrote the throw down as the true thing. That is not what the courtesy means and she has done it that way ever since, for anyone who arrives with hands and no words.

items.name: Tentacle
items.description: A severed coil of violet muscle, suckers still gripping at nothing. Voidmaw has more where this came from.
items.loreDesc: A severed coil of violet muscle, suckers still gripping at nothing. Voidmaw has more where this came from.
loreStory: Cut off, it works for most of a day: grip, slacken, grip, tightening on cloth, on a strap, on whatever else is in the bag. So it travels wrapped alone, and it gets checked before wrapping, because whatever the arm last lay on comes away held in the rings — grit, chips of black rock, a splinter off somebody's crate.

loreStory.t: One came over the counter at the fen market with a reed in the third sucker. Reeds do not grow within two days of the black rock. Either the animal went down into the wet country and came back, which nobody who works that ground will hear, or the ground itself has been somewhere else lately, which is the answer
Gunnar
gives when he gives one at all. The reed is in a box at that market. People are shown it, and then the market gets on with the afternoon.

items.name: Fang Charm
items.description: A fang hung on a leather cord, worn smooth by a thumb. Somebody believed in it right up to the end.
items.waiting_for: a tribe that wears its kills
items.loreDesc: A fang hung on a leather cord, worn smooth by a thumb. Somebody believed in it right up to the end.

loreStory.t: The shine is on the left face of the base, where a right thumb sits when it is not thinking about it, and that is years of somebody.
Solveig

has learned to ask about the charm before she asks the name. You wake in the grass wearing what you wore, and for the first hour most people cannot produce their own name to save themselves — but a man who cannot tell you what he is called will tell you straight off that he won this from his sister's husband, that it is a boar's, that it is not a boar's and he has always known it. Then the rest comes up the rope behind it. A good share of the names on that meadow were fetched out by a piece of tooth on a string, and she has never once said so to the person it worked on.

items.name: Corked Vial
items.description: A corked bottle of something olive and settled. Palehusk took it off a body that had not opened it either.
items.loreDesc: A corked bottle of something olive and settled, sediment on the floor of it. Whoever kept it never opened it.
loreStory: It has stood still long enough to separate out: a clear finger under the cork, olive through the middle, and a floor of sediment that has not been stirred in a very long time. That is the sum of what anyone knows about the contents and it is not nothing. A bottle only settles like that if it is carried level and never once broached. Somebody had this for later, the whole way along a road, and later did not arrive.

loreStory.t: Crackers will not draw the cork, and it is not nerves, it is arithmetic. Sealed, twenty-six gold. Open, it is a bottle. So it goes down the counters exactly as it came off the black rock and out of a
Palehusk
's grip, and every hand it passes through decides the same way, and the thing goes on being for later.
Bettany
has asked three of the buyers who take them what they want them for. Two gave her nothing worth writing down. The third stopped coming.

items.name: Magma Stone
items.description: Faceted like an egg, orange over deep red and split with glowing seams. Fire-things leak these when they crack.
items.loreDesc: Faceted like an egg, orange over deep red and split with glowing seams. Fire-things leak these when they crack.
loreStory: A good one holds its heat nine or ten years and gives it out steadily the whole time, which is more than wood ever managed, and that single fact has ruined a road.

loreStory.t: The west road tried it. Three stones banked in a ring at the old post, glowing all night, no rota,
nobody sitting

— the argument being that the stones did the part of a fire that costs money and the sitting was ceremony. Six years of that. Then the last mile went soft, then the post, and the crews sent out to relight it cannot now agree on where it stood. The stones are still warm. They are sold at the far end as hearth-stones, by a man who does not mention the road.

items.name: Red Plume
items.description: A red plume with a pale shaft, bright as a warning. Whatever wears these does not need camouflage.
items.loreDesc: A red plume with a pale shaft, bright as a warning. Whatever wears these does not need camouflage.

loreStory.t: Red carries at dusk and does not rot, so for a long stretch of years the east road was marked with these: one plume in the verge every hundred paces, on the side that was safe. Somebody walked it twice a year and re-planted the ones the ground had moved. That was a job, with a name and a rota, and it lapsed. The plumes are still out there, most of them, still red, and about a third of them are now on the wrong side.
Wendell
can tell you which third, if you sit with him long enough.

items.name: Crooked Twig
items.description: One dark twig with a knob at the end. Stumpling sheds a hundred a season and misses every one.
items.loreDesc: One dark twig with a knob at the end. Stumpling sheds a hundred a season and misses every one.

loreStory.t: Five gold for a stick. Say that out loud at a stall and the seller will wait you out, because the answer is not funny. Somebody is buying. Everything that comes off anything that walks goes into the same carts sooner or later — teeth, hide, cracked shell, and twigs, by weight, no questions asked about condition. Children on the east road work this out inside a season and keep a sack under the bed. Grown men are embarrassed to be seen stooping, and stoop. The carts go east and come back empty and the drivers are perfectly civil, and not one of them has ever been able to say who pays them, or what for.
The trade
gave up asking a long time ago. The price is good and it has never once gone down.

items.name: Bone Talon
items.description: Hooked grey bone, thick and cracked at the base. Fiends and the glowing dead shed them, and the point stays keen.
items.loreDesc: Hooked grey bone, thick and cracked at the base. Fiends and the glowing dead shed them, and the point stays keen.

loreStory.t: Everything else in a bag can be assigned. This cannot. A grey talon like this comes off an
Ashfiend

, and an Ashfiend's parts are mostly not an Ashfiend's — it wears what it has taken — so the hook in your hand may have grown on something else entirely, one owner ago or four, and there is no test that will settle it.
Hearn

sorts for people coming off the east country, and he works with two bags. One is the animals: this jaw, that hide, named and priced and gone by evening. The other is the pieces with no address. It is not priced and it does not go on the table, and he has never said what becomes of it. He is the last man on that road anybody would press for an answer. The points stay keen in there for years. He mentioned that once.

items.name: Crab Pincer
items.description: Brown, jointed and hooked at the tip. Whatever the swamp blobs swallowed to get it went down sideways.
items.loreDesc: Brown, jointed and hooked at the tip. Whatever the swamp blobs swallowed to get it went down sideways.

loreStory.t: Nothing anyone has met has a hand like this. Jointed twice, hooked at the tip, built to close sideways — and the only place they turn up is inside a fen blob, a
Puddling
that has swallowed something it could not manage.

loreStory: The ferryman at the second fen crossing keeps twenty-one of them in a flour box and has done for seven years, and the point of the box is the sizes. Laid in order they step up cleanly: thumb-length at one end, then a hand's, then a thing you would want both hands to work. Every one of them right-handed. He sells everything else he pulls out of a blob and he will not sell one of these. He will show you the box if you ask. What he says while you look at it is that he would like, one time, to be handed a small one again.

items.name: Curved Fang
items.description: White ivory going tan at the root, worn fine by use. Cave-jaws and dusk-hunters both leave these behind.
items.loreDesc: White ivory going tan at the root, worn fine by use. Cave-jaws and dusk-hunters both leave these behind.

loreStory.t: Six animals leave this exact tooth and on a counter there is no telling which:
Prismclaw
Winterfang
Duskfang
, and three more, and anybody who works that country will give you the other three differently.
Twelve gold, which is what a curved fang is worth when it could be anything. One that somebody watched come out fetches four times that, and the difference is not ivory, it is the watching.
Wendell

put it best with one in his hand at a fire, in the middle of trading what he remembers of the east road for the company of people willing to hear it again: you are not buying the tooth, you are buying somebody who was there. Then he sold them the east road one more time, and they paid him in the same coin, and everyone got what they came for.

items.name: Diamond
items.description: Cut, clear and cold, throwing light in every direction. Whatever swallowed it did not know what it had.
items.loreDesc: Cut, clear and cold, throwing light in every direction. Whatever swallowed it did not know what it had.

loreStory.t: Nothing here cuts a stone like this. What comes out of a creature comes out rough; this has fifty-eight faces and a girdle true the whole way round, and there is no wheel in Nangijala and no shop with the patience. So it was worn. Somebody carried it up out of
the meadow
in a ring or sewn into a hem, lost it in water, and something that swallows bright gravel got lucky.

loreStory: The cutters can date the work — the style, the proportions, near enough the decade. That is the whole of what it will tell you. It gives up a workshop and a fashion and not one syllable about the hand it sat on, which is the ordinary cruelty of evidence: it outlasts the person and then answers a different question.

items.name: Bat Wing
items.description: Dark membrane on thin bone struts, folded shut. Leathery, and off nothing anyone has cornered yet.
items.loreDesc: Dark membrane on thin bone struts, folded shut. Leathery, and off nothing anyone has cornered yet.

loreStory.t: Membrane is the best patch material in the country: waterproof already, takes a stitch without splitting, will not go stiff in cold the way tanned hide does. Boat seams, tent corners, lantern shades. Mostly it goes on bellows, which fail at the fold, always the fold, and a fold lined with wing runs a season past the leather around it —
Sigrun

's has three on it, dark on grey, and she dates her own work by which patch is which. Thirteen gold. The man who sells them will tell you he takes them down himself at dusk, with a long pole. He does not. They are found on the ground, folded shut, one at a time, and he has never seen one in the air either.

items.name: Oak Plank
items.description: Planed dark oak, the grain unmistakable, knocked out of a Stumpling. It walked once, and now it holds shelves.
items.loreDesc: Planed dark oak, the grain unmistakable, knocked out of a Stumpling. It walked once, and now it holds shelves.

loreStory.t: Count the rings on the end grain. There are none. There is grain — beautiful grain, dark and even, straight as a ruled line — and any joiner will tell you a
Stumpling

plank works like nothing that ever grew, because nothing that ever grew is that agreeable. A tree has a bad year in it somewhere, a drought, a neighbour, a season it spent leaning. This has no years in it at all. It is exactly as much wood as a hundred thousand people were sure of, and not one splinter more.

loreStory: The rule on that road is old and worth keeping. Build shelves out of it. Build a counter, a door, a bench for the fire. Do not build a bed. Whatever it eventually takes into its head to do, you want to be standing up when it does it.

items.name: Iron Quills
items.description: A cluster of grey spines, hard as nails and about as friendly. Tuskmaul wears a ridge of them.
items.loreDesc: A cluster of grey spines, hard as nails and about as friendly. Tuskmaul wears a ridge of them.

loreStory.t: Nothing about them is a quill. They are the grey spines off the ridge of a
Tuskmaul

, a hand long, hard enough to pin oak, and the name comes from one man at one fire who split a tip, dipped it, and produced a blot the size of his thumb and a line that gave out after two letters. He has not been allowed to forget it.

loreStory: He is also the reason four fires on that road can read at all. He taught it evenings, for nothing, badly, for about sixty years, and when he comes in for a drink now somebody always sets an inkpot down in front of him, and he always looks at it, and everybody laughs, himself included and loudest.
Thirty gold the cluster. Joiners buy them, not scribes. Iron weeps in that country and a quill never has.

items.name: Red Leaf
items.description: One leaf gone crimson out of season. Thornstag browses and the whole branch dies looking like this.
items.loreDesc: One leaf gone crimson out of season. Thornstag browses a branch and the whole branch ends up like this.

loreStory.t: A
Thornstag

leaves a line of them behind it, crimson in a green month, plain as chalk on a wall, and any fool can read it. Any fool does. What the line gives you is where the animal has been, which is the half of the question nobody was asking. The other half — where it is going — is sold by four or five people who get it by sitting out an autumn night near something worth robbing. The colour keeps for years, which is the second trade in them: a red leaf is the cheapest way to prove to a fire that you have been somewhere.

items.name: Dented Flask
items.description: A traveller's flask, dented flat on one side. Empty, but it still smells faintly of something strong.
