soul.power: +14 shadow damage and 15% chance to fade from sight after a kill

items.loreDesc: Matte black, softly faceted, handing back no light at all. In a full pouch you find this one by touch, not by eye.

loreStory.t: Stones are sorted on a dark cloth by lamplight, and every one says something on the way down — a coin of light, a stripe. This one lands and there is only cloth where it landed. Old hands still count the row twice before tying the bag. The fix is
Sigrun
's: any pouch that leaves her bench with one of these inside has a bright thread sewn to it, no charge, no comment. You check the thread.

Set in a blade it is the not-being-seen, finished and portable. Fights end, and the ending does not particularly include you: the shape goes down looking at somebody else. Off a creature that spent its whole loud life
charging head-first
, that is the stone's one correction — the charge was the noise. The bottom fact was never being looked at.

loreStory: Sigrun also keeps one loose in her apron, unset. A smithy is a place where people stand about and watch your hands, and on the days when the work on the bench is a cracking, she would rather the watching slid off.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Mint-green with a serpent coiled across it, left by a Blightcur. Whatever it carries, it survives.

soul.power: Attacks poison the target for 6 a second, stacking twice

items.loreDesc: Mint-green with a serpent coiled across it, left by a Blightcur. Whatever it carries, it survives.

loreStory.t: Sellers of this one demonstrate before they name a price. The cloth comes off, the stone goes into a bare palm — mint-green, cool, a serpent coiled across the face of it in low relief — and it stays there as long as the customer cares to stand and watch, because a whole class of buyer will not touch one otherwise. This is the useful thing the stone says that
the animal

never will. Sit inside twenty paces of that dog and it costs you something you do not get back. Carry its last hard piece all winter and it costs you nothing, ever, and no handler has yet taken so much as a foul week off one. The sickness was cargo. What reached the bottom was the carrying — which is why a blade with one set in it leaves a wound that goes on working long after the blade has gone elsewhere.
Wendell

owns one, and people find that funny for about as long as it takes him to explain it. He is old and does not walk far, so he is on the short list of people a fire has to be moved for when that line comes round; it has happened to him twice. The young walker who carried his things the second time came back a season later and put the stone on his sill without much of a speech. Wendell could sell it for two winters of firewood. He would rather look at it, because it is the only proof anyone has brought him that one of those rounds ended.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Rough brown rock seamed with raw gold, grazed loose by an Amethyrn. Coin comes easier to whoever carries it.

soul.power: +18% gold found and each critical hit drops 5 gold

items.loreDesc: Rough brown rock seamed with raw gold, grazed loose by an Amethyrn. Coin comes easier to whoever carries it.
loreStory: It does not find gold. Any honest seller says that first and the price second and has no third thing to say. What it does is make you sure. Carry one and you will be certain about the next foot of rock, or about which of two roads has the paying end, in the flat unarguable way you are certain of your own hand — and you will be right often enough that two hundred and sixty gold starts to look like a bargain.

loreStory.t: Often enough is not always, and the men carrying them cannot tell those two apart from the inside. A digger who has been right four times running will tell you he read the ground. He cannot say whether he found the seam or the stone walked him onto it, and by the fifth time it has stopped occurring to him to wonder.
The trade's own line
is that a soulstone does not make you stronger, it makes you harder to argue with. This is the one where that stops being a compliment.
The stone itself is rough brown rock with raw gold standing up in the seams of it, warm, heavy, and workable by no one, so that
the one substance here that never drifts

sits inside the one substance here that cannot be forgotten. Scholars enjoy that a great deal. The diggers have the better observation and it is shorter: certainty is not knowledge, it is only what knowledge feels like from the inside.
Amethyrn
is never wrong about a hill. It is the size of a cart, and it is out east walking around made of the stuff.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Blackened shell webbed with live lava, cut out of a Magmane. A weapon takes its fire and leaves things burning.

soul.power: +22 fire damage on hit and burns the target for 4 per second

items.loreDesc: Blackened shell webbed with live lava, cut out of a Magmane. A weapon takes its fire and leaves things burning.

loreStory.t: The standing argument about
the lion

is whether any of the heat is its own. It is Made, so nothing in it ever lived anywhere else: remembering that gathered at a volcano's throat, thickened, and stood up. And everything on that ground is hot, the boulders included. Stand close and you have stood near a hot animal on hot rock, with nothing in it you can separate.

loreStory: The stone settles that. A blackened shell webbed with live lava, brightest where the webs meet; two hundred and eighty-five gold; and still exactly that hot at the bottom of a pack four hundred miles west, in a wet country, in winter, with the mountain nowhere in it. The heat came away when the stone did.

Off an edge it goes in and stays in: what you struck is still burning while you decide what to do next. That follows from the animal. The fire is shut under the glass and opens only once it has decided about you, and it does not decide twice.

loreStory.t: Sigrun

charges for the iron rather than the setting — a housing that touches a web has to be forged around the stone in place, with the stone in the fire throughout and indifferent to it. She has done four. Over each one she says the same sentence to whoever is paying, in the flat voice she keeps for people who want a thing and would rather not know about it: this will still be doing that when you have stopped.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Grey granite gone green with moss, off a Cragback. It weighs what a hillside weighs, in the hand.

soul.power: +22 armor, and nothing knocks you off your feet

items.loreDesc: Grey granite gone green with moss, off a Cragback. It weighs what a hillside weighs, in the hand.

loreStory.t: You do not go hunting a
Cragback

. You buy a sighting, and a sighting comes from somebody who has stood in one doorway at one hour of the evening for eighty years and can tell you the line of the hill is not the line of the hill. Crews pay for that, by the sighting, in gold, and it is the only work in the country whose entire qualification is having looked at the same thing your whole life without once getting bored of it.

loreStory: What comes out is grey, green in the seams, brown-crusted along one flank, and it weighs what it has no business weighing; handlers take it in two hands without deciding to. Set into armour it makes you hard to get through, which is what the sheet says and not what anybody buys it for. They buy the other half: bridge-holders, the two or three who still stand at the gorge crossings, anyone whose work is being exactly where they were put while something large arrives.

At the bottom of a made thing is whatever made it, and this one was made by a hundred valleys' worth of people agreeing about a hill — the same dark line against the same evening, generation on generation, not one of them ever giving an inch on it. That is the fact in your fist, and it has nothing to do with strength. It is about not being argued out of a position. Two hundred and forty-five gold, and the old man who sold the sighting is back in his doorway at the same hour, learning the new line, because a hill that has moved once is a hill you no longer know.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Mossed plates around a yellow-green star, torn from a Mosscairn. It strikes with growth and knits you as you fight.

soul.power: +10 nature damage and +2 health regeneration per second

items.loreDesc: Dark green plates shut around a yellow-green star, and the moss on them is still growing. It cuts and it mends.
loreStory: The only piece that is still doing something. Set one on a shelf and leave it a year and the moss has got further — a plate's width up the shaded side, on a stone fed nothing and watered by nothing. People who handle stones by the sackful stopped finding that remarkable long ago, and still keep this one where they can see it.

The trade's one argument is where to put it, because the stone does not care. Growth goes into whatever it is set against: turned outward on an edge it opens a shape faster than the shape can close, worn against the ribs it closes the wearer while they are still being opened. Same work. It is not doing two things.

loreStory.t: Hearn

wears his sewn into the lining, ribs side, and has kept it there since before the mountain. His ruling on the argument is the longest sentence most people have got out of him: a thing that cannot tell cutting from mending, you keep on your own side of the fight. He paid
a Mosscairn's
fist for it, and calls the price fair, which from Hearn is a review.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Olive and root-threaded, taken from a Nightmule's stubborn heart. Your blows turn green and your wounds close over.

soul.power: +10 nature damage on hit and regenerates 3 health per second

items.loreDesc: Dull olive under a dark web of root, plain enough to lose in the grass. Your cuts close over and your blows come up green.
loreStory: Stones are weighed by hand before they are weighed by scale, and the hand is hunting appetite: a piece off something that burned sits in the palm with a want that comes through a glove. This one sits there like a stone — matte olive, no shine, easy to lose in grass — and the trade priced it accordingly for years. Wrongly. The flattest ones are not empty; their want is pointed at something other than you.

loreStory.t: Carry one and the pointing shows: by evening the small hurts have closed unnoticed and the day's work has come apart readier than the edge explains. Everything else off a
Nightmule

is about a person who is not there. The stone alone is about the animal, and there is no owner in it at any depth — whoever walked at the front never reached the bottom. What reached the bottom was the going on, unloaded, in a straight line. That is the part in your pocket.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Olive-grey with a fleck of gold buried in the middle. Dunedelver swims through sand and finds these.

soul.power: +12% chance a kill yields a second drop

items.loreDesc: Olive-grey and speckled, with a fleck of gold buried dead centre that nobody has got out. Off a Dunedelver.

loreStory.t: Hold it up and the gold is right there — a few grains of it, a finger's depth inside speckled olive rock with no seam and no crack to reach it by. Every owner tries once.
Gold
is the one substance here that does not drift, remembered identically by everyone who ever handled any, and there is not one account anywhere of a grain of it coming out of one of these.
Osric

tried properly, being a smith and being new enough to take a thing like this for a problem rather than a fact. He gave it a full working day. The stone came up to heat and stayed a stone, the gold in the middle of it stayed precisely where it was, and at the end he had a warm stone and a shop full of people who had come round to watch. It is still on his bench. He says it holds paper down.

What it does in the field is what the animal does. Sand is the one ground in this country that keeps nothing: put a thing under a dune and the dune hands it back, upright and clean, a season later. The stone works the same way on a fight — you take what there is, you finish, you turn away, and now and then the ground gives up one more piece behind you off a thing you were done with. There is no explaining why it should.
The delver
is not looking for anything either.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: An opal shell of soap-bubble colours. Beautiful, valuable, and belonging to nothing anyone has met.

soul.power: +8% dodge, and the first hit each fight glances off

items.loreDesc: An opal shell of soap-bubble colours. Beautiful, valuable, and belonging to nothing anyone has met.

loreStory.t: Two hundred and sixty-five gold on a good day, and the honest sellers will tell you the number is invented. A price in this trade is a story about a creature: how hard it is to find, how hard it is to break the shape, how many crackers walked home. Take the creature out and the floor goes with it.
Gold

is the one substance in the country that never drifts, which is precisely why the drift shows here — the same stone has changed hands at forty and at four hundred inside one season, and both sellers went home pleased.

loreStory: It earns some of that. An opal shell in soap-bubble colours, cells of pink and cyan and gold shut in by fine dark seams, the whole surface moving as your hand turns without one of those colours actually being in it. Worn, the first blow of a fight glances off, and after that you are simply hard to lay a hand on.

loreStory.t: Bettany

keeps a page for it that is nothing but a column of dates. Fourteen sales she can confirm across eleven years, and every one goes back exactly one hand and stops — a buyer who had it from a seller who had it from a man he can describe and cannot name. She gave up for a while, because every seller answers and every answer is true. Then she took it up again. The missing creature does not trouble her much; the rule everyone learns first says there is one, and she can be patient. What troubles her is the supply. They arrive in ones, out of different directions, and they keep arriving.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale opal that holds a crescent whichever way you turn it. Moonpelt's own, and the moon wants it back.

soul.power: +10% dodge at night, and moonlight closes 4 of your wounds a second

items.loreDesc: Pale opal that holds a crescent whichever way you turn it. Moonpelt's own, and the moon wants it back.
loreStory: Every other stone is a fact and works in a tin. This one wants a condition. Indoors it is a pretty object — milky, lilac and mint and cyan moving under the surface, a crescent standing in the seams that stays put however you turn your wrist. Out under open sky at night it shuts a wound while you are still deciding whether to sit down, and nothing gets a clean hand on you.

Which is why the tellers dislike it, and they are not wrong to. The whole of the Keeping is people sitting still in one place with a fire and each other; a stone that pays a man to be out on a road under the moon instead is, put politely, an argument against the rota. Sellers put it the other way round — the fires are far apart now and somebody has to walk between them — and both sides have had their piece ready for years and neither has moved an inch.

loreStory.t: Wendell

walks at night and will not have one in the house. He is pleasant about it and does not lecture, and anyone who has sat with him works out why unaided: every one of these was somebody's payment for breaking a
Moonpelt

, and one of those holds thirty paces behind him over broken ground and comes no nearer than the edge of the light. Watch the animal all night and you can still tell yourself the frost under those paws is the light playing tricks. Carry the stone one night and the argument closes. The not-touching was the last hard thing in there. It is in your pocket, and it is working on you.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Orange stone forked with white light. It hums in sunlight, and no creature yet has answered for it.

soul.power: +18 radiant damage on hit, and burns undead for another 10

items.loreDesc: Orange stone forked with white light. It hums in sunlight, and no creature yet has answered for it.
loreStory: The hum is not audible across a room and never has been. It is in the hand, and only in sun: carry one into shade and it stops inside a breath, take it out and it is back before your fingers close. Two hundred and fifty gold, orange plates forked through with white. In a weapon it burns, and it burns worst at whatever has been longest out of the light.

A man on the western roads has carried one for forty years. He does not fight with it and has never had it set. The pocket has been re-sewn nine times and the stone is exactly as it was the day he was paid it — a stone cannot be forgotten, so it cannot wear, so it outlasts the patience of the man carrying it by a margin that does not bear working out. He takes work that moves. A man who stays where he is meets what comes past him; a man who keeps going meets more.

loreStory.t: What he is waiting for is whatever this came out of, and he has a description ready and no evidence for any of it: something that stands out in the open at the top of the day, something that hums. He has never heard it anywhere but in his own hand. Asked what he means to do if it is ever in front of him, he does not say break it. He says he will do it
the courtesy
— sit down a little way off, ask its name and one true thing. He knows how that sounds. He has known for forty years and has not changed the answer.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Chalk-cream and webbed with fissures, pulled from a Diretusk's ivory. It plates your armor against breaking.

soul.power: +12 armor and immunity to fracture effects

items.loreDesc: Chalk-cream, crazed edge to edge with fine dark fissures, and not one of them gives. In armour it refuses to come apart.
loreStory: Hand one to somebody new and watch the thumb. The whole surface is crazed, fine dark fissures dividing the chalk-cream into panels like a flat of dried mud, and every pair of hands new to it presses, gently, to find out how near the thing is to coming apart. It does not give. The trade keeps a short demonstration for buyers who will not take that on trust, involving a bench and the flat of a hammer, and the stone wins.

loreStory.t: It stays cheap all the same, and the reason is honest: there is nothing to feel. In armour it pays out at the one moment you would otherwise not be getting up, and that is a hard thing to sell to anyone who has never been on the ground.
Solveig

keeps the fire the broken re-form beside, and has sat with what comes back — minus a little of what it was thinking — often enough to have a settled opinion. She gives every new bag-carrier heading out the same advice: past the bright stones, buy the dull one. The ones who laugh at the price have not been on the ground either. She says it pleasantly, once, and does not argue. Her fire will make the case for her some night, whichever stone they chose.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale green plates around a white core, warm as a greenhouse. Nobody has found what grows them.

soul.power: Regenerate 4 health a second, and healing on you is 10% stronger

items.loreDesc: Pale green plates around a white core, warm as a greenhouse. Nobody has found what grows them.

loreStory.t: Solveig
keeps hers in the apron, left pocket, and has done for longer than most of the people on that meadow have been
awake

. What is broken re-forms beside the nearest tended fire, and hers is the nearest tended fire for a long way in three directions, so she has had a great deal of practice at the hour afterwards — somebody sitting in the grass with their hands going, short a little of whatever they had been thinking about. She puts the stone into those hands and holds them shut around it until they can manage a cup. Pale green plates around a white middle, warm the way a glasshouse is warm. It does the rest.

loreStory: Dealers have explained to her, more than once, what she is carrying. That the plates and the white core match nothing anyone has ever broken open. That by every rule of the trade a stone with no shape behind it should not exist. That a collector in the south would pay well for it and ask her nothing. She says that is nice, and thanks them, and goes back to the fire.

Pressed on why she is not curious, she gives the same answer she gives to everything, which is the oldest courtesy there is: you ask a newly woken soul their name and one true thing, and you do not ask where they came from, because for most of them the answer is a hole and the asking widens it. She has never seen why a stone should be handled worse than a person. Seventy-eight gold, forty years, an apron pocket. Her hands are bad in the cold, and it is good for that too.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale grey and full of slow swirls, all a Nightmare leaves. Hold it and you will not recall your dreams.

soul.power: Attacks frighten: the target flees for 2 seconds, once every 12

items.loreDesc: Pale grey and full of slow swirls, all a Nightmare leaves. Hold it and you will not recall your dreams.
loreStory: Every dealer of any standing keeps a book, and every book says the same thing about this one: it comes back. Never for a fault. It works perfectly for as long as you own it, which is the trouble. A fighter buys one, carries it a season, sleeps beautifully, and one morning sets it on the counter and takes two thirds of what they paid without arguing the price. Asked what is wrong with it, they cannot say. Most of them mention the weight.

loreStory.t: That book is harder evidence than anything written down about
the pale horse

itself. Watch it go by and you lose one night and do not miss it — nobody misses what they cannot remember having had. But one stone sold four times in six years out of the same shop, to four people who each thought better of it and none of whom could say why, is a measurement. It says the loss is real in the one place it cannot be felt, and it says so in a ledger, in a hand that was only keeping accounts.
There is one column that never turns round.
Hearn

buys them. Three so far, at the asking price, no haggling, and he has never sold one back; the dealers on that circuit know to hold one for him. He went into the mountain with a party and came out of it by himself, and he has made one statement about the inside in all the years since. He does not appear to need a second.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale green plates, cool and slightly damp. Some creature grows these; the valley has not shown it.

soul.power: +8 armor, and moss and mud never slow you

items.loreDesc: Pale green plates, cool and slightly damp. Some creature grows these; the valley has not shown it.
loreStory: Every stone in the country comes out of the grass warm and stays warm. Handlers grade by heft in the dark and the warmth is how the hand knows it has hold of a stone and not a pebble. This one is cool. Cool and faintly damp, pale green plates with a brighter seam at every crack, and it does not dry out — a dry shelf in a dry room through a dry month, and you pick it up and it is exactly as you left it. Forty gold. It turns up in junk lots between the teeth and the buckles.

loreStory.t: It is the stone people start with, and it is honestly good at what it is for: a whole season of moss and wet clay and slick root, and not once do you go down for footing. Press the graders and they will commit to one sentence, said flatly, on the way to something else — whatever reached the bottom of this spent its life keeping its feet in wet ground. That narrows the valley by about half. It narrows the list of things anyone has ever broken not at all, because this is not on that list. New hands ask. Old hands used to. Somewhere between the two the question aged out, the way questions do here when
the work
is steady and the answer costs money, and the stones go on arriving.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Sun-bleached with a gold heart, wrung out of a Dewling. It makes blows land heavy and leaves them blinking.

soul.power: +8 blunt damage and attacks blind the target for 2 seconds

items.loreDesc: Sun-bleached plates cracked round a heart of gold, all a Dewling leaves. Blows land like a dropped weight, and dazzle.
loreStory: Cutlers keep the seams turned outward, for the flash: whatever takes the hit stands blinking at nothing for a second, and there is no light anywhere about to account for what it thinks it just saw. Bedded the wrong way, it is merely heavy.

The sorters grade them by how little colour is left. A sand-brown one came off ground somebody still walks. The bone-pale ones, seams gone nearly white, come off meadows a great many people remember and none of them visit any more, and fetch double. A strange way to price anything; the trade stopped finding it strange long ago.

loreStory.t: Bettany
came to the sorting sheds last autumn and copied ten years of grade-books into
the Chronicle
, price by price, and would not say what she wanted them for. She did not need to. Anyone can read a column that only climbs: every season the
Dewlings
come up a little paler, off a few more meadows going unwalked.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale blue with a white star locked in the ice, out of a Bergclaw. Cold enough to ache through a glove.

soul.power: +11 frost damage on hit, and hits crack shields: -20% enemy block for 5 seconds

items.loreDesc: Near-white, with a six-armed star standing darker in the ice, out of a Bergclaw. Cold enough to ache through a glove.
loreStory: There is cold, and then there is this. It does not take the chill off a room and give it back; it is exactly as cold in a warm hand as in a snowbank, and after a while the ache comes up through the glove into the wrist and you set it down. Handlers keep them in wool under a wooden lid, grade them by eye, and do not linger over it.

loreStory.t: In a fight it does what frost does to rock. Cold does not shove a hard thing over — it gets inside and opens it. Shields come apart against this, not smashed but opened, and the next blow goes through a guard that was perfectly sound a moment before. The reading is the plainest in the trade: what went to the bottom of
Bergclaw
had learned that ice is not the soft part of a winter.
Solveig
has the other reading and has never offered it to a buyer.
The courtesy

is to sit with the newly woken and ask them their name and one true thing. She has met wakings she could not do that for — animals in the grass, no name to give, nothing to say — and she sits the hour out with them anyway and files it in her head under unfinished. A soulstone is one true thing, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly mineral. This one is ninety-six gold and lives in a tin on a shelf. She has said what she thinks about that exactly once, and not to a buyer.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Granite plates seamed in salmon pink, dropped by a fleeing Fluffang. Armor that shrugs off falls and crushing weight.

soul.power: +15 armor and 10% reduced damage from falling and crushing blows

items.loreDesc: Grey granite plates held by unbroken salmon-pink seams. In armour a crushing blow arrives as a shove, a fall as a bruise.
loreStory: It is not one piece, and that is the trade of it: grey granite plates held each to each by salmon-pink seams, so it holds the way a wall holds — by how it is joined. Struck along a seam it opens into two clean plates that both still work; struck across the grain, gravel. Reading the pink before the hammer falls is a living in itself.

loreStory.t: In armour it makes the ground feel closer: drops come off short, and what lands on you arrives without the part that was going to break something. The trade's sour rule holds here — stones off things that struck go into blades, and the stones that keep a person whole come off
a white creature
that never struck first in its existence, and spent the whole of it on one question: where to be standing when something heavy happens.
Hearn

wore one on the one organised walk anyone ever made on the cave. The others carried striking stones, and ribbed him the whole way east for armouring himself off a rabbit, and he let them. He came back alone, and unhollowed, and has never said whether the stone mattered inside. What is known is smaller: it has not been out of his plate since — not regraded, not repriced, not looked at.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Deep purple veined in gold, heavy as a crown. Unclaimed, which has not stopped anyone hunting for it.

soul.power: +20% gold found, and merchants pay 10% more

items.loreDesc: Deep purple veined in gold, heavy as a crown. Unclaimed, which has not stopped anyone hunting for it.
loreStory: The names a bench uses for what a stone grades to are all borrowed from creatures: frost, ember, storm, grave, blood, moss. Point at the word and you can point at the animal. This one is filed royal, and royal is not a kind of anything — it is the word that got used because the tray needed a word. There is no creature anybody would file under it, which has not stopped two or three crews going out to look, with no description to go on and a price to go on instead.

loreStory.t: It does not cut. It does not burn and it will not hold anyone up. What it does is get you paid: an offer arrives a tenth over what the same bench would have said an hour before, and the man making it cannot afterwards say why, and ground you have walked twice gives up
gold
on the third pass. Nearly everything else on the shelf is an appetite or an endurance. Pressed to the bottom of this one is an expectation of being owed.

loreStory: Deep purple plates, thick gold in the seams, and heavy — nothing that size has any business sitting in a hand like that. Two hundred and seventy-five gold, a number arrived at by merchants, in a room, with one of these on the table. Twice a year somebody proposes a blind price: the stone in a box, in another room, valued by people who cannot see it. The proposal has never once been carried, and the men who vote it down are the men holding one.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Cracked dark rock veined with live red, still warm from the Emberjaw. It sets whatever you strike alight.

soul.power: +12 fire damage on hit and burns the target for 4 per second

items.loreDesc: Dark plates split by live red, brightest where the seams meet. It never cools, and what it sets alight keeps burning.
loreStory: A bag of hard pieces can be sorted in the dark if one of these is in it. Every soulstone comes out warm; this one comes out well past warm and stays there, year on year, with nothing going in. Carriers keep it wrapped and away from their backs, because after a day of it you stop being able to tell which of you is the warm one.

Setters grade by depth, against a strong light. Red that stops at the skin of the plates lights what you strike and has done; red that runs down in keeps it lit after you have moved off and stopped attending. And it will not divide — split one along its own cracks and you hold two dark rocks and no fire — so the hilt is built around the whole of it.

loreStory.t: A cracker once offered
Jehanne

a deep one for her rota hearth: set it in, the fire never goes out, walk the circuit in half the nights. She refused it flat, and the refusal is the nearest she comes to a creed — a fire that keeps itself is not a fire. The stone can burn. It cannot sit with anyone. She walks the full circuit still, and the coal off
the crusted thing on the black rock
goes into sword-hilts instead, where burning past reason is a virtue.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale blue and rimed white, all that survives a Frostling's melt. Hits land cold and sometimes drag the target down.

soul.power: +10 frost damage on hit and 20% chance to slow the target

items.loreDesc: Grey-blue plates, white rime in every seam, cold to hold. All a Frostling's melt leaves; its hits leave a target wading.
loreStory: The only cold hard piece. Every other kind sits at blood heat within a breath of being picked up; this one stays cold for as long as anyone has troubled to hold it, and the sorters use that as the test — blue junk warms in the hand while you are still asking after it, a real one never does.

loreStory.t: The price is not about the stone; it is about the walk. The high snow lies a long way above the last fire anybody still tends, and a collector broken up there — usually by the very
Frostling
they were working — comes back together beside the nearest fire still kept, which is most often
Solveig's
on the meadow, a full day's climb below the morning's collecting, still lying in the drift where it fell.

loreStory: Solveig has learned the look of it: somebody assembling out of the fire-warmth at noon with snow still in their idea of themselves. She puts the kettle on and does not ask. By evening, as a rule, they are talking about going back up. Not many go up twice in a season. She has never once asked the ones who do.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Brown stone threaded with living roots, taken from a Gnarloak. Leave it on soil and it takes hold.

soul.power: Regenerate 5 health a second, and hits root the target in place for a moment

items.loreDesc: Brown stone threaded with living roots, taken from a Gnarloak. Leave it on soil and it takes hold.
loreStory: It travels on a plate. Every dealer who carries one keeps a plate for it, or a board, or a square of slate, and every apprentice is told the reason and finds it out anyway: set it down on bare soil at dusk and by morning it has taken. The stone comes up unharmed — it cannot be harmed — but you have spent an afternoon with a spade and lost a flagstone, and the man who sold it to you will not be sympathetic about either.

So there are places where somebody put one down and never came back for it. A soulstone cannot be forgotten and does not decay, so it is still there, rooted, and will still be there when the road that used to pass it has gone somewhere else. People build to those. A fire ring on the west road is laid around one, and the keepers' argument — whether the ground under it holds because of the stone or because of fifty years of people coming back to sit at it — will not be settled, and both sides keep coming back to sit at it.

loreStory.t: In a fight it takes a thing's feet for a moment, and that is the joke, and the trade tells it badly and often.
The creature
was assembled out of everyone's memory of a tree going over, and its last hard piece hands the axeman the one still moment he wants.
Osric
will set one for anybody who asks, at the ordinary rate, same as a buckle. He does not keep one in his own tools, and if you ask him why he will talk to you about hafts until you stop asking.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Rust-brown and rough as an old hide, taken from a Tuskmaul. Warbands have broken against less.

soul.power: +15% maximum health, and shoulder charges cannot be interrupted

items.loreDesc: Rust-brown and rough as an old hide, taken from a Tuskmaul. Warbands have broken against less.
loreStory: It is the one stone in a bag you can find by touch in the dark. Everything else in there comes up smooth or seamed or glassy; this is rough the whole way over, pitted and creased like a hide left out for a century, and it sets badly — it wears through leather, and a haft has to be cut deep to hold it. It does not make a person stronger. It makes them impossible to stop: once you are moving, nothing arriving from the side gets a say, not a blow, not a shove, not the ground.

loreStory.t: Then the part worth sitting down for. There was an age here with people enough in it, and agreement enough between them, to put a shield-wall in a field and walk it forward in step. They walked it into
the old bull

, and the wall is the part that broke. Everyone in that line re-formed beside some fire the same night, short a little of what they had been thinking, and went home, and their age went the way ages go. The agreement is gone. The wall is gone. What is left of that field sits on a bench with a price against it, warm, rough, and entirely uninterested.
Jehanne

was offered one at cost by a fire-keeper who owed her, and said no, and gave her reason at the fire that evening: a shield-wall is a rota, only larger and in a hurry, and she would rather have the rota. She keeps one. It has two names on it. It has had two names on it for a long time.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Old iron gone sour, weeping copper from every slit. Quillkin leavings, and they rot armor right off a foe.

soul.power: +9 damage on hit and reduces the target's armor by 6 for 8 seconds

items.loreDesc: Near-black, slit all over, bright copper standing in every slit. Blows land harder and the armour that stops them fails.
loreStory: New hands rub the copper on a cloth, expecting the orange to come away. It never does — the first sign this is not rust in the ordinary sense — and it is warm, which rust is not. The trade grades on the copper regardless: bright, and running the full length of the slits, is a prime one; brown and pinched out is a dry one, and a dry one does noticeably less to the other man's armour.

loreStory.t: The odd part is that no two carry the same rust. One kind of animal, one kind of stone — there is no argument about that part — but one comes up coppery, one near black, one with a green in it, and the difference is not the animal. What pressed down in here is iron that was never its own: somebody's left-out things going off in the weather, year over year, beside
a small kept appointment
Wendell

was handed a green-tinged one at the fire a few winters back and turned it in the light a long time. The green, he said, was paint; he could name the gate it flaked off, and the wall the gate hung in. Then he talked until the fire was low, and for once — ask anyone who knows the old man — he named no price.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Scorched dark red with embers sulking in the cracks, the last of a Slagling. It warms your blade and your hide.

soul.power: +4 fire damage on hit and 10% burn resistance

items.loreDesc: Scorched near black, embers banked in every crack. A Slagling's last warmth: it warms the blade and the hide behind it.
loreStory: Most hard pieces go into the bag. This one goes into a pocket, and a great many never come out again: the seams stay lit, a low orange banked down in the cracks that has never yet been seen to go out. In a blade it is a poor bargain and the trade says so — the edge runs a little warm, and that is the whole of it.

loreStory.t: The quarrel about them is old and fair. A teller will point out that warmth is not
a fire

— a fire is warmth with somebody talking beside it — and the two ought not to be confused. The ones who walk the black rock, where the rota lapsed further back than anyone can date and the nearest tended fire is a day down the mountain, answer that up there a warm thing in the pocket is not an argument about anything. It is company.
Jehanne
keeps fires for a living and a
Slagling's
ember in her coat, so both sides of the quarrel claim her. She lets them. A woman who prays without believing has room, she says, to be right in both directions.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Green plates around a glowing core, shed by a Sporehorn. The fungus is steering the stone as well.

soul.power: Hits release spores: 10 poison damage a second in a small cloud

items.loreDesc: Dark green plates around a pale glowing core, out of a Sporehorn. The fungus is steering the stone as well.
loreStory: It is the only stone sold with instructions, and the seller says them out loud whether or not you want them. Do not seal it. Do not set it flush. Leave the back of the cup open, keep it somewhere light gets at it, and if the plates lift, let them lift.

loreStory.t: Because it is not finished. A soulstone cannot be forgotten and so cannot decay, and this one is not decaying — it is doing the other thing. Dark green plates stand slightly proud around a pale core that makes its own light, and over a season they stand a little prouder. What took
the elk

took it from the antlers down and did not stop at the bottom of it. Set it in a blade and every hit opens a small cloud that keeps working in the air behind you, which is the entire ambition of the thing steering it: arrive somewhere, and then be there.
Osric

argued about the instructions. He was a smith before he woke and he still counts in living years, and a fitting that is required to stay open offends him at a level he cannot talk himself out of, so he sealed one properly, brass over the back, to prove a point. It went dark inside four days and stayed dark. It still fights, a little. He keeps that one in his apron and brings it out when a customer wants to know why his settings cost what they cost, and he does not enjoy the demonstration as much as he pretends to.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Deep violet scattered with white specks, dropped by a Duskhoof. Like it, the stone casts no shadow.

soul.power: +12% dodge in darkness, and standing still in shadow hides you outright

items.loreDesc: Deep violet scattered with white specks, dropped by a Duskhoof. Like it, the stone casts no shadow.
loreStory: Put one on a windowsill in the sun. Everything else on that sill lays a shadow; beside this there is a clean bright place where a shadow should be and is not, and it will go on doing that all day, on any sill, for anybody who cares to stand and watch it. That is what makes the thing worth a hundred and fifty gold, and something else besides. It is not a story about an animal at dusk in poor light told by a man who has had a drink. It is a stone on a plank, and it holds.

On a person it works the way it works on the light. Stand still in shadow with one on you and you are not hidden so much as declined: eyes arrive, then find somewhere else to be, then go back to whatever they were doing. Moving in the dark, hands miss. Sellers state this plainly and buyers ask twice anyway, because it does not sound like a thing a stone should be able to do to a person.

loreStory.t: Sigrun

sets stones into steel for a living, and there is one she hands back. She takes it out of the cloth, looks at it as long as anybody does, and says she has enough work on. There is a black horse in her yard that hauls charcoal and leans its whole weight into her hand of an evening; every one of these fell out of an animal like
that one

; and she knows better than anybody at that fire what it is to put a stone into a piece of steel and then swing it every working day for the rest of your life. She has not explained herself. She is not going to.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Night-black and star-flecked, prised out of a Balefiend. Void-heavy hits, and now and then you blink in behind.

soul.power: +22 void damage on hit and 10% chance to blink behind the target

items.loreDesc: Night-black, small lights all through it, pale seams branching over it that open into nothing. Lighter than it should be.

loreStory.t: Handlers grade stones by heft in the dark, and this one lies to the hand: night-black, full of small lights at no settled depth, and far too light for what it is. It is the dearest thing the eastern ground gives up, and it is paid for in
gold
only — for this one, no seller takes anything that drifts.
Osric

, who had been woken about a year and still thought like a living smith, reasoned that a stone which moves a fighter might move him out of harm's way, and set one into a breastplate. It moved him one stride — into the middle of what he was backing away from. He re-formed beside
Solveig
's fire a night later, short the end of the argument he had been winning, and
Sigrun
pried the stone out of the dented plate, set it in a blade, and hung the plate on her wall where customers can see it.
In a blade, where it belongs, blows land heavy and dark, and once in a while the fight turns and you are standing on the far side of it, facing a back — the side
the Balefiend
was always on: the one you were not watching.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Sand-gold and cracked like a dry bed, left by a Sunscale. It keeps the desert's noon inside it.

soul.power: Attacks flash bright: 15% chance to blind the target for 2 seconds

items.loreDesc: Sand-gold and cracked like a dry bed, left by a Sunscale. It keeps the desert's noon inside it.
loreStory: Every hard piece comes out warm and stays warm. This one keeps a clock: cool enough to forget at first light, awkward by midday, and at the top of the day it will make you shift it off your hip — the same rise and the same fall, in a pocket, in a bag, in a cellar with no window. Sixty-two gold. Handlers who work by touch have told the hour off one and been right.

The heat does nothing; the heat is only what it is. Every so often a blow arrives as light instead of force, a white flash off the sand-gold plates, and whoever was looking at you cannot for a moment. It was never meant to last. Two seconds of somebody else's eyes, priced at the bottom of the sheet with the stones sold to people on their first road.

loreStory.t: Which is a failure of imagination about what is in it. People have followed
the animal

for years and come home with a colour. Nearly every stone on a bench is an appetite or an endurance — a thing that wanted, or a thing that would not stop. This one is neither. It is a way out. The plates were never armour; they were a trick played once, at the correct hour, by something whose whole answer to everything was to not be there afterwards.

loreStory: The crews who work the sand country carry one apiece and will tell you it is for the flash, which is true. Not one of them has ever said what they were doing at the moment they were glad of it, and every one of them has been glad of it.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Dark stone webbed in gold thorns around a green heart, off a Thornstag. Flowers die near it, indoors.

soul.power: Attackers take 12 thorn damage, and your hits slow them by 20%

items.loreDesc: Dark stone webbed in gold thorns around a green heart, off a Thornstag. Flowers die near it, indoors.
loreStory: It lives outside, on the sill, in a stone box. A dealer who forgets loses whatever was in the room with it — cut flowers in one night, then the herbs strung over the stove, then the pot by the window — and the standing test for a true one is exactly that and nothing cleverer. A cut stem laid beside it until morning. Sellers hand you the stem themselves. A proof that costs a flower is a cheap proof.

loreStory.t: Dark, gold-webbed, no trouble at all to grade. Whatever comes at you comes away torn and slower, and does not get its pace back while the fight lasts.
The stag
browses a plot down to dirt and the plot stays dirt, that year and after. One fact to a stone, pressed until it is nearly a mineral, and the fact in this one is about things not coming back.

The part worth looking at costs nothing extra. Turn it to the light and the middle of it is green — a plain grass-green heart, the same green as the stone of any leaf-eating animal on the same bench, and every thorn in the thing worked outside it. Something in that wood used to browse and mind its own business. There is no account anywhere of a Thornstag that did not read as a hole cut out of the dark: not in
the Chronicle

, not from the oldest teller anybody has been able to produce. A hundred and sixty gold, and the green middle is the entire evidence, and it cannot decay, and it cannot be forgotten, and nothing further can be added to it.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: A violet stone with one open eye that follows the room. Gloompard is counted in eyes like this.

soul.power: +15% critical chance from behind, and a kill hides you in smoke for 3 seconds

items.loreDesc: A violet stone with one lidded, slit-pupilled eye that follows the room. Gloompard has four. Its stone has one.
loreStory: The argument at the black-wood fires is the count. Four, say the people who have met it lately, and they are not wrong. Two, say the oldest heads, who learned it before those people were dead. Six, says a man on the north side who is believed about most other things. It never settles, because everyone who has ever counted was in the dark and frightened at the time.

loreStory.t: Put the stones out on a bench and the argument does not end, it changes shape. Every one of them has one eye. Not a mark resembling an eye — an eye, lidded, slit through the middle, open, and tracking the room. Whatever
the animal
has been given out there, what went all the way down was a single one. A drawing is somebody's bad evening. A hundred stones in a row are a count.
Wendell

learned it with two, and gets told at the fire, kindly, that he has it muddled. He puts his stone on the table when that happens. It does not prove his number and he knows it does not; it proves the number went on from outside, that the fire has been adding to it for centuries, and that whatever the table is correcting him about, it is not the animal. He likes the quiet that follows better than he would like being right, and company is what he came for.

loreStory: What a buyer gets, once it is set, is the other half of the meeting: the blow that lands from behind because nothing turned to meet it, and the few seconds afterwards where the smoke has you and the field does not.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Violet with a dark mouth of a core, cut out of a Voidmaw. Set it down and the light near it goes first.

soul.power: +18 void damage on hit, and 10% of it feeds your own health

items.loreDesc: Violet and grey, a live burn of colour at the core, cut out of a Voidmaw. Set it down and the light near it goes first.

loreStory.t: The handlers who work the eastern ground know two stones that ought to be the same stone and are not.
The cave's

comes out cracked edge to edge with nothing in the cracks, because there was nothing left in that shape to settle. This one comes out whole: violet and grey, rough as slag, dense, heavy, with a live burn of colour at the middle that no part of a stone has any business having. That is the entire body of evidence, and it is worse than the guides' tidy answer. Something reached the bottom of
the thing

, which means there was something in there to reach the bottom of. Whatever opens that mouth is not an emptiness walking around inside a body. It is a somebody, at some level, with an appetite and no face to hang it on, and the people who take stones off that ground say so without hedging while the guide-writers go on filing it where it has always been filed.
Somebody put one in a pouch with a
banded solar stone

, as somebody was always going to. Neither stone was any different afterwards — they cannot be, that is the one thing everyone is sure of about them — but the hand's width of air between the two went out and stayed out for as long as they travelled together. Carried into a fight it takes, and hands back a tenth of what it takes, which is more than any other stone hands back to the person holding it. Nobody has ever called that generous.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Violet stone cut with an unbroken knot. Scholars want it; nobody can say what died to leave it.

soul.power: +18 arcane damage on hit, and -12% spell cooldowns

items.loreDesc: Violet stone cut with a knot that has no end. Scholars want it, argue over it, and cannot say what it fell out of.

loreStory.t: People bring this one to
Jehanne

to be read. Not valued — the scholars do the valuing, and they have bid it past two hundred and fifty on the strength of what it does, which is simple enough: whatever you can do, you can do again sooner, and it lands harder than it did the first time. What they want read is the figure. Deep violet, cut clean through with an interlace that crosses itself four times and closes, no end anywhere in it and no place where it begins.

loreStory: She tells them the same thing every time and it costs her a little more each time: it belongs to no rite she keeps, it is in none of her books, and she cannot say what it means. They keep coming. Belief is thin in this country and the appetite underneath it is not, and a closed figure looks so much like something meant that a man will carry it a day's walk to be told what. She knows precisely what she is being used as. She does it anyway, which is the whole of her.

loreStory.t: Asked a fourth time in one evening she once said more than she intended. A figure like that, she said, is what you get when a thing has gone the same round long enough that it has stopped needing anyone at the far end of it — then she got up to see to the fire, and she has not repeated it since. It is still the only reading anyone has offered, and no grader will put it on a card.
The rule everybody learns first
says something was going round. Nobody in the trade can produce it.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Violet, forked white to the shell, dropped by a Stormcrown. The air near it tastes like a coming storm.

soul.power: +22 lightning damage on hit, and criticals arc to a second target

items.loreDesc: Violet, forked white to the shell, dropped by a Stormcrown. The air near it tastes like a coming storm.

loreStory.t: The sceptics' line about
the stag

is older than most of the people saying it: a tall thing on a summit in bad weather gets hit, and that is geometry, not character. A rod with legs, and the rest is people wanting a story out of a hill.

loreStory: The stone is the answer, and not the one they wanted. A stone carries one fact and no more, and this one's is not a thing that was struck. It is a thing that was come to. Violet plates forked white to the shell, working out from a white middle, and the hair lifts on your forearm the moment you take it up. In a fight it does not count one body a finished job: the hit lands, and then it is in the next thing along, and then it has done.

Two hundred and seventy gold, and the rest of the cost is the part nobody prices out loud. The weather that brings the lightning is the weather you have to stand in, so being broken up there is part of the errand rather than a mishap in it, and what re-forms beside the nearest tended fire is short a little of whatever it had been thinking. Ask a seller how he came by his and the answer is honest, cheerful and incomplete, and he does not know it is incomplete.

A stone cannot be forgotten. Everywhere else in the trade that is a remark about value. Up there it means something narrower: whatever else goes out of a man's head on the way down, the stone in his fist is the one part of the errand that comes back entire.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: White stone branching with gold light. It belongs to something that has not walked into the world yet.

soul.power: +16 radiant damage on hit, and undead near you cannot heal

items.loreDesc: White stone branching with gold light. It belongs to something that has not walked into the world yet.
loreStory: White going to pale blue, and the gold in it does not behave the way gold behaves in other stones. It does not lie in the seams. It branches — out of a pale middle, thinning as it travels, stopping mid-run with the ends left fine as hair. Everybody who picks one up arrives at the same word inside a minute, and the word is unfinished.

That argument is over and nobody enjoyed how it ended. Two graders on the north bench set one against a careful drawing of the same stone made ninety years before and went over it line by line, and not a hair's width had moved. Which is what a hard piece does. It cannot decay, it cannot be forgotten, and it does not become anything. So it is not growing toward something. It is finished, and exact, and it is a complete record of a kind of creature that no bench in the trade has ever put a shape to.

loreStory.t: Gold

is the one substance every dead person out of every century remembers identically, and a soulstone is the one thing here that cannot be forgotten at all, and there was never any reason for those two facts to end up in the same object. They are in this one, branching. Two hundred and eighty gold, and it moves slowly, to one sort of buyer: somebody who has decided to go east and would rather not say so aloud. Near it, what has been emptied does not close itself up again, and that is worth the money to them. The sellers' line — that it belongs to something which has not walked into the world yet — is repeated on every road, costs nothing, and has never been an answer to anything.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: Pale as packed snow, pebbled all over, dropped by a Snowmane. It walks beside whoever is lost.

soul.power: +10% movement speed on snow and ice, and cold never slows you

items.loreDesc: Pale as packed snow, pebbled all over, dropped by a Snowmane. It walks beside whoever is lost.
loreStory: It will not sit on a bench. The whole surface is pebbled — packed rounds, like snow squeezed in a fist, each with its own small shine — so there is no flat anywhere on it and it goes off the edge of any table it is put down on. Sorters keep them in a cup. No other stone has a habit of leaving.

Fighters do not buy it, and the price says so: it is the cheapest honest stone anybody sells. Snow stops slowing you, cold stops counting, and that sounds like nothing until you are up where the drifts are with the last tended fire a day below you. The people who own these are carriers and rota-walkers and the ones who work the high snow for other kinds of stone, and the trade knows without saying it aloud that the cheap thing has got more people home than any of the dear ones.

loreStory.t: There is no way in it, whatever buyers keep hoping. What reached the bottom of
the white horse
was keeping to somebody else's pace, for as long as it takes, in weather that ought to make that impossible.
Sigrun

is a weaponsmith and will not put this one in a weapon. She sets them into boot-buckles, staff-ferrules, the tongue of a belt — evening work, and she does not charge for it — and if pressed says only that it is not blade material. She has one stone set in the head of a hammer and has had it there a long time. She is the last person in this country who needs the difference explained to her.

items.name: Soulstone
items.description: White stone cut with a frost-rune that keeps its edge. Its creature is still out there somewhere, unmet.

soul.power: Attacks slow the target by 25% for 3 seconds

items.loreDesc: White stone cut with a frost-rune that keeps its edge, and nothing anyone has ever broken was carrying it.
loreStory: A soulstone cannot be worked. Not scribed, not faceted, not ground down; the trade established that early and expensively, and a setter's whole art is holding a stone fast without altering it by a scratch. Which leaves an awkward question standing over this one, because there is a frost-rune on it.

Nobody put it there. Take one to a window: no tooling anywhere, no bench marks, no chatter in the strokes, and the white star does not lie on the surface. It goes in. It is still going at the middle, and its edges are as sharp as the hour it dropped out of a broken shape into somebody's hand. It is not a mark made on a stone. It is the shape of the thing all the way down, the way plates are the shape of the plated ones. Something is a frost-rune the way a hedgehog is spines, and what it does is entirely in character: whatever it touches runs late.

loreStory.t: Gunnar

asks. He maps ground that will not hold still and is used to figures that refuse to add up, so for years he has put two questions to every seller holding one — where did this come from, who had it before you — and written the answers down. Thirty-one entries. Plotted, they make a scatter with no centre, right across the valley, thinning toward nowhere, which is not the shape a creature's range makes on a sheet. He was asked at a fire once whether he thought there was one out there. He said a scatter with no centre is what you get when you map a thing being handed about rather than found, and did not say the next sentence.

lore.name: The Waking
lore.summary: You died. Then you woke on a meadow, and a stranger was already walking toward you. This chapter is about her, and about the ones nobody got to meet.
body: Nobody remembers the door. You were somewhere else, at the end of something, and then you were lying in meadow grass with your face wet and the smell of woodsmoke coming from somewhere close, and every person who has ever lived in Nangijala began exactly there — on that meadow, within sight of that small stone house, within reach of that fire. The country has one gate and it is a field.

body.t: You will not know your own name. This frightens people more than the dying did. The name is not taken; it just does not always survive the crossing, and a woken soul will sit in the grass for an hour reaching for it the way you reach for a word you have used all your life. Which is why the first thing you see here is not the sky and not the house. It is
Solveig
, already walking toward you, because she watches the grass the way sailors watch weather, and she can tell a waking from a trick of the wind at three hundred paces.

body: She will sit down a little way off, so you can look at her or not. She will tell you what happened to you, plainly, once, because she has learned that kindness with the truth left out has to be done twice. And before you sleep she will ask you for your name, if it has come back, and one true thing about yourself, and she will listen to your answer like it is the only thing happening in the world. It is not a ritual, though it has been done a hundred thousand times. It is the oldest medicine this country has, and you will learn why it works soon enough.

She was not the first to keep that watch. The fire on the meadow is older than any person now tending it, and the ones who kept it before her are a story she will not tell on a first evening — partly because you are not ready, and partly because one part of it she cannot tell without stopping, and she does not stop while she is on watch.
Here is the part she will tell you, because you have to know it and it is better from her than from the wall of some tavern. Sit down for it.
Not everyone comes.

People die together — in the same water, on the same road, in the same winter — and one of them wakes on the meadow and the other never does. Husbands arrive and stand up already scanning the grass for a wife who died eleven years before them, and she is not here, and she was never here, and no one can say where else there is. The woken keep lists. They describe faces to Solveig, to travellers, to anyone who has walked far: have you met her, she would have come the year of the great storm, she laughs before the joke is finished. There is a whole quiet economy of people asking, and the country has never once produced an answer — only the fact, repeated until everyone stops asking out loud: some of the dead never wake, and nobody knows what that means, and everybody is afraid that somebody does.

So when you stand up out of the grass, understand what the woman at the fire is actually doing. She is not staffing a gate. Every waking she meets is somebody's answered prayer — the person a hundred strangers have described to her, finally face-up in the grass — or else it is one more day that somebody's person did not come. She meets you anyway, full-hearted, every time. Ask her how she bears the arithmetic and she will feed the fire and say the watch is the watch.
Welcome to Nangijala. You are dead, you are expected, and you are — this is the strangest part, and it takes everyone a season to believe it — not at the end of anything.

lore.name: The Age of Coming
lore.summary: The ruins of the first age had owners: a lighthouse lit for a brother who never woke, a mill brought by a woman who hated it, a face nobody can ask about — and then the first wall went soft.

body.t: Walk east from
the meadow

for an afternoon and you will pass under a broken aqueduct, through a ring of standing stones, past a windmill with its sails still rigged, and along a line of poles strung with wire that runs from nowhere to nowhere. None of these things belong in the same world. All of them are here.

body: The dead arrive from everywhere and every when, and here remembering is not a private event: a thing held firmly enough, long enough, in enough minds, simply is. Somebody woke knowing exactly what an aqueduct was — knew it the way you know the stairs of your childhood house — and so there is an aqueduct. The oldest call that first stretch of the world's history the Age of Coming. No maintenance, no scarcity, nobody yet suspecting that anything needed keeping; the country grew larger, stranger and more beautiful, and nearly everything good to look at dates from it. But the ruins are not the lesson. The lesson is the people they belonged to. Meet three of them.

The lighthouse stands in the shallows of a sea no ship has ever crossed, and a man named Nils built it with his hands. In life his brother drowned within sight of a real one — lamp lit, keeper awake, the whole machinery of warning working exactly as intended, and his brother slipping under quietly a little way outside the light. Nils died years later, far from any coast, and woke on the meadow still listening for water. On a shore with nothing to warn he built a lighthouse anyway, and then he changed what a lighthouse is for: he lit it every evening, so that if his brother ever woke in this country — on the meadow, in the far hills, anywhere — there would be a light on the water that meant: come here. I kept it burning. His brother never woke. Nils lit the lamp anyway, every evening, for longer than most countries last, because he would not agree that it was for nobody. The lamp is cold now. The tower stands.

The windmill nobody turns was brought by a woman who hated it. She had been put to it as a girl — wind, grain, the same circle of sky — and she walked out of its shadow the day she was grown and never once looked back. She lived, she grew old somewhere with pavement under her feet, she died, she woke on the meadow. Within a season the sails stood up over the birches, because the Age of Coming never asked what you loved. It asked what you knew all the way to the bone, and what she knew, under everything she built on top of it, was the mill. She spent a long age here in its shadow, furious. You do not choose what comes with you. You are not asked.

And out on the ice there is a statue with a face nobody recognises. It was carried here on somebody's back, the whole way, over years; people still tell of the carrier on the roads, bent double, refusing carts, refusing company, setting the burden down at dusk and sitting opposite it in silence until dark. Nobody asked. Asking felt like putting a finger in a wound. Now the carrier is long gone from every road, there is no one left to ask, and the statue stands in the ice being the most important face in somebody's world — name unknown, story unknown, kept upright, the old ones say, by the wondering itself, because ten thousand travellers asking whose face is that, at ten thousand fires, is also a kind of remembering. Whoever it was is held in the world by strangers. That is either the loneliest thing in this chapter or the kindest, and nobody has settled it.

The age ended without ceremony. A man had set a triumphal arch in a field, for a victory won in a country that is not here, and for a long lifetime he told that victory to anyone who slowed down — until one year he stopped, because everyone had heard it. The carved faces on the arch went smooth first, like wax near a flame. Then a wall somewhere was not as tall as it had been, and then it was a heap, and then a green place where a heap used to be. Whole streets began to be less. Nobody understood. They blamed the winters, they blamed the ground, and there was a whole confident generation certain it had something to do with the sea.

body.t: It had nothing to do with the sea. The answer was paid for by one silent woman, and what it cost her is
the Age of Fires

lore.name: The Age of Fires
lore.summary: Signe learned the world's rule by losing Emil to her own silence. The first fire, the rota as an apology to a boy who cannot hear it, and the argument between telling and writing that nobody has won.
body: Before the rule had words, somebody paid for it. A woman called Signe woke early in the world's history, when the country was young and nobody yet knew it needed keeping, and the first thing Nangijala ever gave her was the sound of her boy laughing on the far side of the meadow. Emil. He had gone through the ice at seven; she had carried that for years, and then followed; and here he was, running at her through the grass, still seven, still hers.

Signe was not a talker. That is the whole tragedy in one line. She loved enormously and said almost none of it, on the old reasoning that a thing said aloud gets smaller. She sat with her boy inside a silence she believed was full. Love that says nothing had never cost anyone anything.

Then Emil began to thin. Slower to name things, at first — the stream became the water, and then he only pointed. Then slower to be named: neighbours' eyes went past him, and a traveller once asked Signe, kindly, whether she lived alone. She did what silent people do. She gripped harder and said less. She held his hand on every walk and told nobody so much as his name, because saying it aloud would have made it real.

body.t: He went
Quiet

holding her hand. There was no moment to point to. The hand was in hers, and then the hand was empty, and the place where he had been was slightly wider than it should have been. She had lost him twice now. The second time was her fault, and the fault was silence, and she did not know either of those things yet.

body: She did not speak for a season. It began as mourning and ended as the coldest experiment this country has ever run: while she sat in it, the world went soft around her. The path they had walked lost its far end. The gate he had swung on stood less certainly on its hinges. Everything nobody spoke of was leaving, and she recognised the weather — it was the one that had taken her son. The discovery was not an insight. It was an autopsy.
The things people talk about stay.
And the half of it that was hers to keep: a boy who went through the ice at seven is talked about by his mother, or by nobody.

So she lit a fire, because you cannot make people sit and listen in the dark and the cold, and listening, it turns out, is the whole medicine. Then the woman who had said almost nothing across two lives sat a stranger down and told him about Emil — the winter, the ice, what his voice did to a room — until her own voice went, and the stranger listened until it was done, and around that one fire the world firmed up like ground after frost. What is told aloud, to somebody listening, holds. It was the world's one law, found too late for the only person she wanted it for.

body.t: What grew from that evening is called the Age of Fires, and it was the best of us. Fires, and a rota: somebody answerable for every fire, somebody walking the circuit between them carrying names, somebody meeting every waking to ask a name and one true thing while somebody else listened. They call the whole of it the Keeping. And every part of it — the rota, the fires, the questions
Solveig
asked you at
your own waking
— is Signe's apology to a boy who cannot hear it. This country runs on love that arrived too late and refuses to stop arriving.

The argument came later, and it has a knife in it. A told story grows — retold a little warmer, a little braver, a little better shaped, by people who mean nothing but well. Keep a man alive by telling him for forty years and you have a man: solid, present, going nowhere, and not quite the man who fell. The Fire-Keepers call that the price. So the Chroniclers said: write him down, exactly, once, and he is safe from all of you and your warmth. They were right and thorough —
the Chronicle
is their book;
Bettany

writes it now — and then they found the thing nobody has explained. A person recorded perfectly goes Quiet anyway, on the usual schedule, beside their own complete and accurate account. It was never the accuracy, the Fire-Keepers say; it was the listening. That is not an explanation, the Chroniclers say; it is a slogan. Nobody has won. You will be asked.
As for Signe: she never forgave herself, and she never
went on

. Late in her age, people who knew her said the two had grown into each other until she could not tell them apart — staying had become the apology. Then the record thins, the way records here do, and what became of her is not written. Not in this book. Not in any teller's round. The woman who taught the world its keeping was not, herself, kept.
But the fire on the meadow — the one you woke within sight of, the one
Solveig

feeds tonight — has never once been let go out. Underneath everything this country still does, every name asked and every true thing listened to, there is a woman saying to a boy, too late, in the only language she ever managed: I am still here.

lore.name: The Quiet
lore.summary: Nothing here dies. It thins — Bright, Faded, Habit, Quiet. You learn the stages the way everyone does: from outside, beside Wendell on the east road, visiting somebody who is no longer home.
body: You cannot die in Nangijala. That door is behind you and it does not open twice. The newly woken find this reassuring for about a season.

It does not mean nothing can happen to you. You can be broken — knocked past the point of holding a shape — as unpleasant as it sounds, and not an ending. What is left of you goes where the remembering is thickest, in practice the nearest tended fire, and puts itself back together beside it over a few hours. You keep what you were carrying. You lose a little of what you were thinking about. Nobody here treats a fight as final, and everybody knows exactly how far it is to the nearest lit fire.

body.t: What can still happen to you is slower, and a list of stages will not teach it to you. You learn it watching somebody you love. So learn it from
Wendell

, the oldest head at the meadow fire, who pays for his suppers with the east road — the carts, the inn at the ford, the summer the verge came up in flowers, all from when the road was safe. People trade him a listening for an evening of it and think they are being kind to an old man. Then, when the weather is quiet, Wendell walks that road himself, out past where anybody goes now, to visit somebody.

body: Thinning has four stages, called the same four things since anybody started counting: Bright, Faded, Habit, Quiet. None of it hurts. That is the part people find hard to hear.

Bright is what you are now. You know who you were and you can say it — your name, your work, the face of somebody you loved, the road home. The one he visits was Bright a long time. She told the east road better than he does; he learned it from her. He does not say what she was to him. Nobody asks twice.

Then you Fade. The particulars go first, so gently nobody catches them leaving. She knew she had loved people; she could not produce the faces. She knew the road went somewhere, and no longer which way it ran. A Faded person is still entirely present, with less and less to say about it, and it is the stage where saying them back to themselves, out loud, at a fire, still takes. Wendell did that for years. Some evenings it worked, and those were the worst ones, he says, because of what they let him hope.

Then there is Habit, where it stops being sad and starts being frightening: the person is gone and the behaviour is still running, a shape walking its round with nobody home. She walks the east road now. The same stretch, out and back, at the hour she always walked it. Wendell falls in step beside her. He gives her back her own stories at walking pace, the carts, the ford, the flowering summer, and she does not stop, and he does not stop either, and when the light goes he stands still in the road and lets her walk away from him.

body.t: Count what the old man is doing before you call it sentiment. A shape at Habit holds only as long as its round holds, and a road nobody speaks of goes soft like everything else. So he sells the east road to the fireside, one listening at a time, keeping it firm under her feet. And he walks beside her so that anybody who comes out that way with a hammer, meaning the quick mercy the trade deals Habit shapes, finds an old man standing in the road first. What the trade does is
the next chapter
. Wendell has read it. He has an opinion about mercy.

body: Carry her with you among the wild things, because nearly everything out there is at Habit too. The creatures are not wicked. Some outlasted their occupants, some never had one at all, and either way they come at you for reasons that stopped being reasons long ago — a round still walked, a bridge still guarded for a keeper whose name went out of the world before it did. Do not hate them. Every one of them is somebody's east road.

And at the end, the Quiet. The shape lets go. There is no body and no grave, because there was no death; the thing simply stops being anywhere, and afterwards the place it was seems slightly wider than it should. People who have watched say the worst part is how ordinary it looks. Wendell has watched. The worst part, he says, is that the road will still be there.

The Quiet is what this world is afraid of — not the creatures, not the cave, not the winter. Every fire, every rota, every supper an old man buys with a dead road is the same answer to the same question. Nobody says the question out loud. It walks the east road on the quiet evenings, at the pace of an empty shape, an old man keeping up, saying carts, saying ford, saying flowers.
Who is going to remember me, and will they do it out loud.

lore.name: The Hard Pieces
lore.summary: What a soulstone is, and the trade's two words for taking one — told through Sigrun, who released her own husband rather than let a stranger crack him, and has not said his name since.
body: Everything that thins gets thinner all the way down, and then stops. At the very bottom one thing refuses to go any further, and if the shape is broken open it falls out into the grass. It is about the size of an egg. It is warm.

body.t: This is a soulstone. It is not a soul — a soul is a whole person, and no person fits in a stone. What is in there is the last piece: one fact, one appetite, one habit of being, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly a mineral. A thing that spent itself burning leaves a stone that is still, in some stubborn way, about burning. A thing that endured cold leaves a stone that endures it. One kind of creature, one kind of stone, no exceptions — except near the eastern mountain, where what the broken things leave behind is
another matter

body: Because a soulstone cannot be forgotten, it cannot decay, and in a country where everything else is quietly going soft that makes it the most valuable substance there is. Work one into a blade or set it into armour and it lends you a little of what it remembers. It does not make you stronger. It makes you harder to argue with.
